News.title: Fresh foreign aid farce as £13m of taxpayers’ cash helps Mozambique sell gas while Brit families face soaring bills
News.content:
MORE than £13million in UK taxpayer cash is helping Mozambique profit from flogging ­natural gas.

It comes despite new drilling being banned in the North Sea, stopping Britain from getting similar returns.



The Foreign Office has funnelled money to the East African state to help it better collect revenues and manage finances.

The project was set up in 2018 to ensure Mozambique state can “reap the imminent benefits of gas revenues”.



The UK gets no return on its investment.

The £13.2million Tax and Economic Governance Programme runs until at least the end of 2026.

It could instead fund annual energy bills of nearly 9,000 struggling British families or restore £300 Winter Fuel Payments for 44,000 pensioners.

Mozambique is soon set to rake in around £4.6billion a year from selling gas and taxes on firms operating in its territory.

Critics slammed the double standard and called for Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to scrap the deal.

Reform’s Robert Jenrick said: “This is nuts. Reform will slash foreign aid and get drilling again in the North Sea.”



The Foreign Office said: “The Tax and Economic Governance programme helps prevent money-laundering and strengthens Mozambique’s ability to identify and remove funding that could be directed to terrorist groups, protecting the UK both at home and abroad.”

News.title: Man, 75, dead & woman rushed to hospital after fire rips through building as at least 3 others left needing treatment
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FIRE TRAGEDY Man, 75, dead & woman rushed to hospital after fire rips through building as at least 3 others left needing treatment

A 75-YEAR-OLD man has died with a woman raced to hospital after a horror fire tore through a building.

At least three other people were treated for smoke inhalation at the scene after the blaze broke out at a property on Ridgway Road in Shelton, Stoke on Trent.

Emergency services, including an air ambulance, scrambled to the property where they found the elderly man dead.

The building was evacuated and fire crews eventually managed to extinguish the flames.





The force are working with Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service to establish what started the fire.

Police added that the man’s next of kin have been informed and his family are being supported by specialist officers.

They are appealing for any witnesses to come forward.

A spokesperson for Staffordshire Police said: “A man has sadly died and four others suffered smoke inhalation following a fire in a property in Shelton.

“We were alerted to a fire by colleagues at Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service in a property on Ridgway Road at around 12:50pm today.

“Fire crews extinguished the fire quickly and the building was evacuated.

“Sadly, a man aged 75 was found deceased and four others were treated for smoke inhalation, with one woman in her 60s being taken to hospital.

“The next of kin have been informed and are being supported by specially-trained officers.



“A scene has been set up whilst we work with fire investigators to determine how the fire started.

“Anyone with information about the fire should call 101 quoting incident 432 of 8 August.”

News.title: Strait of Hormuz could soon reopen as deal between Iran and Oman looms, US official claims
News.content:
THE Strait of Hormuz could soon reopen as a deal between Iran and Oman looms, a US official has claimed.

They said progress was made in talks between the nations, which sit on either side of the Strait.



A deal between Iran and Oman over control of the strategic ­waterway is seen as crucial to a wider peace agreement in the US’s five-month war with Iran.

The official, who did not want to be named, said: “There is progress between Oman and Iran, and we expect a deal soon.



“Once it is announced to restore commercial shipping without impediments, the United States will lift the blockade of Iranian ports.”

Before President Donald Trump and Israel launched the war on Iran, about one in five barrels of oil consumed worldwide went through the Strait.

But Iran has fired on ships that try to cross without permission.

Meanwhile, Lebanon and Israel have agreed on a shortlist of countries to ­verify the disarmament of terror group Hezbollah.

It is part of a US- brokered deal to end the war in Lebanon.

News.title: It’ll be a disaster if early release scheme isn’t halted – child abusers, wife beaters & cop killers must stay locked up
News.content:
ANDY Burnham’s first act as prime minister has been to approve the early release of paedophiles, grooming gang members and killers – like the killers of Andrew Harper – from prison.

Labour have finally U-turned on releasing rapists, but only after weeks of pressure from Conservatives, campaigners and victims.



It is a relief that they have – but you need only look to the despair of PC Harper’s widow, Lissie, to see this is only a very partial victory.

Labour’s Justice Secretary, Alex Norris, actually apologised to her on the very day the new exclusion for rapists was announced, knowing that her husband’s killers would still go free.



On the same day, the Prime Minister had the gall to say he felt the victims’ pain.

Burnham and Labour have completely misread the public mood.



Most of us think killers, rapists and paedophiles already serve sentences that are too short.

Now, thousands will be released after serving half or as little as one third of their sentence.

We are told the public will be safe because of advanced tagging and strict licences, but we know that recalls to prison are up 28% and offenders are breaking their licences consequence-free – last year one prisoner released early went 50 days without a tag before anyone noticed.

Labour’s ex Prisons Minister, Lord Timpson, shockingly said it was impossible to know exactly which criminals would be released, where, or when.



Calculations by the Conservatives revealed that 9,300 domestic abusers stand to be let out early, and over 350 criminals guilty of manslaughter.

We are told that only “less serious” child abusers will be released early – what kind of child abuse is “less serious”?

Victims’ rights campaigners are rightly outraged.

We are told the Government has no choice.

But they said that before – and then they conjured up a thousand spaces to stop rapists being released.



If they were not telling the truth then, why should we believe them now?

Analysis by my party shows there are 4,000 usable prison spaces the Government could use.

It is wrong that criminals who have killed police officers should be set free. There are only two of these eligible for early release in the prison estate. Two.

Are Labour really saying – having just found 1,000 slots – they can’t find room for those who have taken the lives of police?

And Labour are not even building the spaces they say they are. When you factor in prison cells that are being mothballed or labelled unfit for purpose, the number of available places in prison actually fell by 400 last year. They say they are building prisons faster than ever before – it’s just not true.



Burnham has so far failed to tell us how he is going to stop rapists being released. Parliament isn’t currently sitting, and they need to change the law to stop this before it starts. We have called on Labour to pass an emergency law the day Parliament comes back.

But when we have asked them to spell out the plan, we have had silence. They must push back the start of the release scheme and use the time to change the law as a matter of urgency to keep dangerous criminals behind bars.

A disaster is unfolding as dangerous criminals are set to be let back onto our streets. But despite asking repeatedly, Labour won’t tell us the plan.

How long before a released killer strikes again, and we are all grieving over yet another tragedy?

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It would cost Labour nothing to act quickly to ensure criminals who have killed our brave police officers are kept behind bars. They risk their lives every day for our safety – it’s the least they can do to show gratitude and care for them, and for their families.



Burnham must keep child abusers, wife beaters, grooming gang members and cop killers locked up – where they belong.

News.title: ‘Coronation Street’ rapist’s cause of death confirmed after vile predator died aged 69 while locked away in prison
News.content:
SERIAL PREDATOR ‘Coronation Street’ rapist’s cause of death confirmed after vile predator died aged 69 while locked away in prison

THE cause of death for the “Coronation Street” rapist has been confirmed after the vile predator died in prison.

Andrew Davies was aged 69 when he died earlier this year while serving out 13 life sentences for a spree of horrific crimes throughout the 1980s in Greater Manchester and beyond.



Davies, who died on February 28, died from natural causes after contracting brain cancer, a report from the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman has disclosed.

He largely carried out his attacks in the Manchester area and became known as the Coronation Street rapist because his victims mainly lived in terraced houses in the north of England.



The predator would often break into the homes of victims and use weapons to threaten them, and in one case caused injury, before assaulting them.

Davies, who was locked up at Category C prison, HMP Moorland, was set free after 34 years behind bars but was recalled just six weeks later after breaching his licence conditions.



Prior to his release, the Parole Board rejected an application from then Justice Minister and Deputy PM, Dominic Raab, to cancel his scheduled release.

He was recalled just six weeks later after breaching his licence conditions and his application for parole was denied in 2024.

The report reads: “In October 2017, Mr Andrew Davies was sentenced to life imprisonment for sexual offences.

“He died of brain cancer on 28 February 2026, at HMP Moorland.



“He was 69 years old. We offer our condolences to Mr Davies’ family and friends.

“The Ombudsman’s office wrote to Mr Davies’ next of kin to explain the investigation and to ask if they had any matters they wanted us to consider. They did not respond.”

The statement added: “They found no factual inaccuracies. At the inquest, held on 8 April 2026, the Coroner concluded that Mr Davies died from natural causes.”

His death has come as a relief to his victims, with one telling Manchester Evening News it was a “very difficult feeling to handle”.

In 1987, Davies had raped her in her own bed at knifepoint and she said “I still relive what he did to me”.



He also attacked a 26-year-old woman in her Sheffield home while her terrified three-year-old daughter hid behind a settee.

In 1988, he was sentenced for raping 11 women and slapped with 11 life sentences with an additional 56 years for other offences.

He was then handed an additional two life sentences in 2010 and 2017 respectively for rapes he committed in 1981 and 1982.

News.title: Teen, mum & grandma die after tourist helicopter crashes & sparks huge fire as devastated family watched on from hangar
News.content:
FOUR people have been killed in a horror helicopter crash during a birthday trip for a teenage girl.

Three members of the same Colombian family and the pilot died when the Robinson R44 helicopter crashed in the Vista Chinesa region, south of Rio de Janeiro.



Harrowing footage shows firefighters battling to reach the still-burning wreckage as flames engulfed the aircraft.

All four people on board were killed in the resulting blaze.



Firefighters were called to the scene shortly after 11am, with 40 emergency personnel and 11 vehicles sent to the crash site.

But rescuers faced a treacherous operation, with the helicopter coming down in a steep, wooded area surrounded by cliffs.

The victims have been named as grandmother Rocio Cubillos, 59, mother Wendy Manrique, 37, and daughter Sofia, 17.

The pilot, Alessandro Rocha, was also killed.



Rocha was reportedly an experienced pilot with more than 20 years in the industry.

He is survived by his partner and three children – two boys and a girl.

The three Colombian tourists were reportedly on their first trip to Brazil.

They arrived on Monday and were due to remain in the country until Tuesday.

According to relatives, the family booked the helicopter tour after researching operators on social media.



Rocio’s son, Vitor Manrique, his wife Daniela Castañeda and their 15-year-old daughter were waiting for the family to return at the hangar.

The family had booked the helicopter ride to celebrate the teenager’s birthday.

They became alarmed after hearing an employee say there had been a “forced landing”.

The relatives said they repeatedly asked staff what had happened, but were given no information.

They eventually learned of their relatives’ fate through news websites while they were still waiting at the hangar.



Lieutenant Colonel Fábio Contreiras said rescuers faced major difficulties reaching the crash site.

“The biggest challenge for the teams right now is access, both to enter and exit the site,” he said.

“The aircraft crashed in a very steep, wooded area with precipitous cliffs, where it is only possible to work using rope techniques and safety equipment.”

He added that a fire had broken out following the crash after the aircraft’s fuel ignited.

“When we arrived, in addition to the helicopter, there was also a fire caused by the explosion of the aircraft’s fuel. That fire has now been completely extinguished,” he said.



“Now, our challenge is to find faster access routes to facilitate the work of the Civil Police and Cenipa forensics teams, as well as the future removal of the bodies.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The exact cause of the crash remains unknown.

The Brazilian Air Force said an investigation is underway to establish what caused the helicopter to come down.

News.title: Women will be killed as a result of Government’s ‘unsafe’ early release scheme, probation bosses warns
News.content:
PROBATION bosses are warning women will be killed because of the ­Government’s “unsafe” early release scheme, The Sun on Sunday can reveal.

The union Napo, which ­represents probation and court staff, has also declared no ­confidence in the Prison and Probation Service.



Bosses are now balloting on strike action after slamming PM Andy Burnham and Justice Secretary Alex Norris in a message to members.

Mr Burnham has been forced to roll back parts of the “unfit” release programme after a public backlash.



Serious sex offenders including rapists will now be excluded from the plan.

But there will be no change to manslaughter cases — meaning two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper’s killers are due out.



Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole will be eligible to leave prison after serving half their sentences.

A petition against the thugs’ early release has passed 810,000 signatures.

In total, from next month the number of offenders monitored by tags, which are overseen by ­probation workers, will hit 40,000 — up from 28,000 earlier this year.

Ministers are now said to be looking at further U-turns in the first major scandal of Mr Burnham’s premiership.



Napo says the reversals do not go far enough, warning in a major intervention that ministers have failed to “address the real issues of public and safe releases”.

The union wrote to members: “The Prime Minister and the Justice Secretary have failed to ­acknowledge the probation workloads crisis that has afflicted the service for over two years.”

A senior union source said “plans to release thousands of domestic abuse perpetrators and stalkers early” mean “more people, largely women, will be killed or harmed”.

Ian Lawrence, Napo’s General Secretary, told The Sun on Sunday: “Everyone is talking about prisons, and yes it is bad, but the crisis in probation is far worse. But yet again, our members are being overlooked while all the attention is on prison.”

Shadow safeguarding minister Alicia Kearns told The Sun on Sunday: “Probation officers are the last line of defence between dangerous men and the women they target. When they warn Labour’s early release scheme will get women murdered, every minister should be shamed into acting to protect us. Scrap this scheme now.”



The Ministry of Justice said “Our record £700million investment in probation and community punishment is ensuring staff have the resources and powers to manage offenders safely in the community.”

News.title: Andy Burnham suggested FORCING  private landlords to sell rental homes just months before becoming PM
News.content:
ANDY Burnham suggested private landlords should be forced to sell their rental homes just months before becoming PM.

He called for more “public control” of housing so that properties could be made energy-efficient “quickly” to meet green targets.



Speaking at an eco-summit in March when he was Mayor of Greater Manchester, Mr Burnham said: “We can, if necessary, take homes out of the private rented sector and put them into the public housing stock so that we can give people homes that are cheaper to rent and cheaper to run.”

Shadow energy minister Andrew Bowie said: “Under the guise of Net Zero, Andy Burnham wants to send officers of the state to your door and take your home.



“We should just make electricity cheap and let people choose what works for them, rather than threatening repossession.”

Sources said Mr Burnham was specifically talking about Manchester and that his ideas at the time are not government policy.



Under Mr Burnham, Greater Manchester set a target of carbon neutrality by 2038 which includes steps to improve homes.

He also previously called for private rental properties that do not meet legal requirements in the Decent Homes Standard to be bought by councils through compulsory purchase orders.

News.title: Met Office issues fifth heatwave verdict as 33C scorcher forecast on Sunday
News.content:
Met Office issues fifth heatwave verdict as 33C scorcher forecast on Sunday

The Met Office has forecast a fifth UK heatwave with temperatures set to reach 36C in East Anglia and south-east England by Thursday.

View 2 Images Heat health alerts have come into force (Image: PA)

Parts of the UK are bracing for a fifth heatwave next week, with temperatures forecast to soar as high as 33C on Sunday.

‌



Yellow heat health alerts came into force at 9am on Saturday as the mercury climbed throughout the day, hitting up to 28C across the South and South East, and reaching 27C across much of central England.

‌



According to the Met Office, Sunday will bring spells of rain to Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, with isolated showers possible in the South East.

‌



However, the rest of the country will remain largely dry and sunny, with most people experiencing temperatures well into the high 20s.

With yet another heatwave on the horizon, health officials have issued warnings about the risks of taking certain medicines in hot weather, including ibuprofen, as they can make it harder for the body to stay hydrated, regulate temperature or cope with sun exposure.

Dr Alison Cave, chief safety officer at the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, said: "Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), commonly used to treat acid reflux and heartburn, have also been linked to a very low risk of a lupus-like skin reaction triggered by sun exposure, and common painkillers such as ibuprofen and naproxen may also increase sun sensitivity."

‌



The Met Office warned that southern and south-eastern regions could see the mercury climb into the 30s, with the South East potentially reaching a scorching 33C. According to the Fire Severity Index, any wildfires that break out on Sunday across almost all of east and south-east England are likely to be exceptionally severe.

"Exceptional" severity represents the index's highest possible rating.

The Met Office data, which takes into account rainfall, temperature and humidity, is used by agencies to assess how severe a fire could become should one ignite. It does not, however, indicate the likelihood of wildfires breaking out.

‌



The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued yellow heat health alerts covering the East Midlands, West Midlands, South East, South West, East of England, Yorkshire and the Humber, and London.

These yellow heat health alerts are set to remain in place until 9pm on Tuesday.

View 2 Images Heat health alerts have come into force (Image: PA)

‌



They caution that the scorching weather is likely to impact the wellbeing of the general public and place additional strain on healthcare services.

The Met Office has warned that heatwave conditions are expected to return next week, with temperatures of up to 36C forecast in parts of East Anglia and south-east England by Thursday.

Two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June resulted in more than 2,800 excess deaths, while two further heatwaves in July have contributed to drought and wildfires.

‌



The National Trust is urging people to sign a petition calling on the Government to make tackling climate change a national mission.

This follows a series of wildfires across the UK in recent weeks, with significant blazes recorded at Dunwich Heath in Suffolk, Headon Warren on the Isle of Wight, Llanwonno in the Rhondda Valleys, South Wales, and the Cairngorms National Park in Scotland. Reservoir levels across England have fallen to 69%, dropping from 72% the previous week and sitting nearly 12 percentage points below the long-term average for this time of year, the Environment Agency announced on Friday.

Levels stood at 85% at the end of June, which matched the typical average for that period, but have been steadily declining in recent weeks.

Article continues below

Five reservoirs are now classified as having "exceptionally low" levels: Blagdon in Somerset (54% full); Clywedog in Powys, which supplies water to central and north-west England (62%); the Dove group of reservoirs in Derbyshire (74%); Hanningfield in Essex (60%); and Wimbleball in Somerset (50%).

Last month was the driest July for England and Wales since records began in 1836, according to provisional data published by the Met Office.

Nineteen counties across England recorded virtually no rainfall - 1mm or less - throughout the entire month, Met Office figures reveal.

News.title: Iran issues Trump 'surrender document' with nine conditions to reopen Strait of Hormuz
News.content:
Iran issues Trump 'surrender document' with nine conditions to reopen Strait of Hormuz

The nine conditions were reported by Iranian media and come as Tehran insists the strategic waterway will remain closed until Washington "corrects its behaviour"

View 2 Images Iran has called the document a "surrender" (Image: Getty)

Iran has set out nine conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, including $300 billion in compensation, the pullout of US forces and a ban on American and Israeli vessels in what it called an "American surrender document".

‌



The nine conditions were reported by Iranian media and emerged as Tehran insists the strategic waterway will remain shut until Washington "corrects its behavior".

‌



Iran's Supreme National Security Council stated the country would "never compromise" either in conflict or negotiations, and that the US must fulfil its conditions before the Strait could fully reopen.

‌



Among the demands are an end to US threats against Iran, a permanent cessation of American military action against Iran and its regional allies, the lifting of the naval blockade and the withdrawal of US troops.

Tehran is further demanding $300 billion in compensation for war damage, the removal of all sanctions and the unconditional release of frozen Iranian assets.

The conditions reportedly include Iran being permitted to levy up to seven per cent on cargo passing through the Strait, while US and Israeli vessels would be prohibited. Ships found to have violated the terms could face a 20 per cent "violation toll".

‌



View 2 Images Donald Trump speaks from the Oval Office (Image: Getty)

The conditions include:

An end to U.S. threats and insults A permanent end to U.S. wars against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen, and Iraq 3.Lifting the naval blockade and withdrawing U.S. forces $300 billion in compensation for war damages Lifting all sanctions Unconditional release of all frozen assets Iran's right to charge up to 7% on cargo A ban on U.S. and Israeli vessels A 20% violation toll on ships if conditions are breached

‌



The remarkable demands follow Iran and the US reaching a memorandum of understanding in June that included plans for the eventual reopening of the Strait and a proposed $300 billion reconstruction fund for Iran. Nevertheless, the most recent Iranian stance indicates that substantial obstacles remain unresolved.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has meanwhile declared that Donald Trump's military strategy has fallen short, asserting that neither the US nor Israel managed to bring Tehran to its knees.

The IRGC characterised the emerging arrangements as an "American surrender document", claiming they highlight Iran's resilience on the battlefield and its negotiating strength.

Article continues below

Trump told reporters on Thursday that he believes the conflict with Iran is drawing to a close, pledging that petrol prices will fall once the war concludes.

He said: "I think it's going to end pretty soon. I don't think they can go much longer."

He further revealed that he is actively engaged in talks with Tehran. "I think we're doing fine," Trump said.

News.title: Voters say mental health support over benefit cuts is best way to get young back into work
News.content:
Voters say mental health support over benefit cuts is best way to get young back into work

EXCLUSIVE: The survey for More in Common found the most popular measure for getting young people with mental health conditions back into work is to increase access to support

View 2 Images Over a million young people are currently out of work, education or training (Image: Getty Images)

Voters believe faster access to mental health support over cuts to benefits is the best way to get young people back to work.

‌



The finding in a survey for More in Common pollsters comes ahead of a major report into fixing the ‘Neets’ crisis by the former Labour Cabinet minister Alan Milburn in the autumn. New Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also declared it a “mission” to reduce the over one million 18-24-year-olds not in employment, education, or training.

‌



According to the survey shared with The Mirror, a majority of all voters believe many young people are out of work because it is too easy to claim benefits instead of working. But the conclusion was not shared by 18-24-year-olds, the results show.

‌



Andy Burnham kicks off summer tour of UK to hear from voters on cost of living READ MORE :

View 2 Images Ex-Labour Cabinet minister Alan Milburn is leading a review of Neets (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

A majority (51%) of respondents in this age bracket said many were out of employment due to mental health problems genuinely preventing them from working. The survey also found the most popular measure for getting young people with mental health conditions back into work is to increase access to support.

‌



Respondents were asked to select up to two responses, and the statement with the largest share on 40% was faster access to mental health treatment. Other options including requirements to look for work, more support from employers, and reducing benefits, all came in joint second on 30%. Just over 22% said better training and qualifications.

Alongside the report into the ‘Neets’ crisis, Sir Stephen Timms, the DWP minister, is also expected to publish a separate review on reform of Personal Independence Payments (PIP) this autumn. He warned last month the main disability benefit, which was introduced in 2013 to help towards the extra costs of disability and support independent living, was “not fit for purpose”.

It was ordered last year after ex-PM Keir Starmer was forced to rip up plans to slash £5billion from sickness and disability benefits in the wake of a major Labour rebellion. UK director of More in Common Luke Tryl said: “The public don’t need convincing that there is a real problem with young people and worklessness.

‌



“Nearly two in three Britons say many young people are out of work because it has become too easy to claim benefits, and a majority say the bigger problem with PIP is that it is going to people who do not need it - a view shared by nearly half of Labour’s own 2024 voters. The public has an appetite for reform to get the benefits bill down.

“ But while the public agree with that diagnosis, their prescription is not simply cuts, but often greater support. Asked what would do most to get young people with mental health conditions into work, the answer chosen most often is faster access to mental health treatment - ahead of tougher conditions or reducing what people can claim.”

“That is the balance Burnham’s Government may need to tread as the Timms Review reports this autumn. Britons want a welfare system that gets people back to work, but they also want to ensure that mental health support is there for those who need it.”

Article continues below

Writing for The Mirror earlier this week - as the government announced the next phase in the roll-out of new mental health units - Mr Burnham also warned of “a profound mental health crisis impacting younger generations”. But he added: "There are those who are quick to criticise young people today, but that’s never been my way. Our country’s future depends on them – and they will have this government’s support.

“The overwhelming majority of the one million young people not in education, employment or training want the chance to build their future. But poor mental health, combined with a system that can’t keep up, robs them of that opportunity. These new NHS facilities will help get lives moving again.”

::: More in Common polled a representative weighted sample of 3,384 GB adults between July 31 and August 2, 2026

News.title: Andy Burnham kicks off summer tour of UK to hear from voters on cost of living
News.content:
Andy Burnham kicks off summer tour of UK to hear from voters on cost of living

EXCLUSIVE: Prime Minister Andy Burnham tells The Mirror he'll be spending the month 'out of Westminster and into your town' to ask people 'what would actually make your life better?'

View 3 Images PM Andy Burnham is expected to spend the rest of the summer on the road (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham is set to kickstart a summer tour of the country this week and ask voters directly: "What would actually make your life better?"

‌



The new Prime Minister, who returns from a short holiday abroad this week, is expected to spend the rest of August on the road visiting every nation and region across Britain. In the coming days he is also set to outline measures to tackle misleading discounts and rip-off prices while promising action to get high streets thriving again.

‌



Mr Burnham told The Mirror: “This month I'm out of Westminster and into your town. Not for the photographs, but because I want to hear directly from people in their communities. I'll be asking one question: what would actually make your life better?

‌



View 3 Images Andy Burnham reintroduced the £2 cap on bus fares in his first week as PM (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

“We know a lot of the issues. People have been saying it for years and no one listened. Bills that land like a threat. A high street of shuttered units and rip-off prices.”

He added: "So here is what's coming. A third off bus fares. VAT off your electricity bill. Action next week on misleading discounts and pricing tricks. We're putting money back in people's pockets and giving communities the power they need to thrive. Good growth in every postcode. Hope in every heart.”

‌



As he returns from a short summer holiday this week, Mr Burnham is expected to renew his focus on the cost of living and travel around the nation before Parliament returns in early September. Insiders confirmed among the places the new Labour leader will visit will be Port Talbot, south Wales - an area reeling from over 2,000 job losses after the closure of a final blast furnace.

Reports have previously suggested Mr Burnham could head to parts of the country where his party has lost support in recent years including areas that voted Reform in 2024. No10 said he will sit down with families, shop owners and workers during the tour.

The visits will ultimately inform his work on a new 10-year plan for the country that Mr Burnham promised later this year in his first speech as Prime Minister. He said at the time it would lay out a “path from where we are now to where I believe we all want Britain to be” later in 2026.

‌



It follows a policy blitz in his first week in Downing with measures designed to give cash-strapped families breathing space on the cost of living. This included a promise to remove the VAT charged on electricity bills from October 1 - estimated to cost £850million - to knock £45 off the average bill.

There was also the decision to reintroduce the £2 bus fare cap to slash day-to-day travel costs for millions of passengers across England from January. The £2 cap was first introduced by the Tories in 2023, but funding was only put in place by Rishi Sunak ’s government until the end of 2024.

View 3 Images Andy Burnham at No10 North in Manchester during his first week as Prime Minister (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Ex-Chancellor Rachel Reeves hiked it to £3 as she battled to balance the books. The current cap, which applies to around 5,000 bus routes across England, was planned to last until March 2027.

In his second week as PM, Mr Burnham also began to grapple with some of the thorniest issues facing Britain including the broken social care sector, defence spending, and the staggering number of young people out of work, education and training. The PM has established No10 North in Manchester which Downing Street said was set up to get the government out of the Westminster bubble.

The summer tour - expected to begin this week - also comes amid evidence of a “Burnham bounce” in the national polls and closing the gap on Nigel Farage ’s Reform UK. Elections expert Professor Sir John Curtice told the BBC last week it was confirmed by Labour's comfortable victory in the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election, where Reform had been hoping for a major political upset in Labour's traditional heartland.

Article continues below

Sir John added: "Polls conducted in the last week put Labour on average in the mid 20s. It is the party's highest standing since the beginning of last year and compares to their rating of 19% in late June when Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down. But with Reform polling only narrowly behind Labour, Burnham's party still has a long way to go before it can face the prospect of fighting a general election with confidence."

News.title: Man accused of Brit's suitcase murder in Greece 'turned back on faith' before her death
News.content:
Man accused of Brit's suitcase murder in Greece 'turned back on faith' before her death

The body of Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was discovered in a suitcase in a derelict building in Athens on July 18, and Afghan refugee and Christian convert Sharif Ahmadzai has been charged with her murder

View 4 Images Sharif Ahmadzai, who is suspected of killing Elisabeth-Jane Ross, and his wife Alaina Hall (Image: FACEBOOK)

The man accused of killing British woman Elisabeth-Jane Ross, who was found dead inside a suitcase in Greece, reportedly “turned his back on his Christian faith” before her death.

Afghan boxer Sharif Ahmadzai has been charged with homicide with intent over the death of 38-year-old Elisabeth-Jane, known as Lisa, whose body was discovered inside a suitcase in a derelict building in Athens on July 18.

The claims about Ahmadzai's faith and behaviour before Lisa's death have been reported by the Daily Mail, which spoke to two evangelical Christians who said his wife Alaina Hall had confided in them about concerns she had regarding her husband's changing behaviour.

According to the newspaper, Alaina told the pair that Ahmadzai had become more distant from his Christian faith and was spending more time boxing and with friends. The sources also claimed she had become concerned about him spending time in bars in Athens.

View 4 Images Elisabeth Jane Ross, also known as Lisa, was found by a homeless man on July 18 (Image: Facebook)

Ahmadzai fled Afghanistan in 2016 and is understood to have converted to Christianity after meeting Alaina through charity work in Greece. The couple run a charity called Love Every Nation, which supports homeless people and refugees in Athens.

Lisa had also been carrying out charity work in Greece as a Christian aid worker and had met Alaina through volunteering and church meetings. Alaina told investigators she and Lisa had become friends after meeting in February.

She reportedly told police she last saw Lisa on July 12. When she later asked her husband when he had seen Lisa, he allegedly said they had last spoken on July 15, when Lisa had asked him to accompany her while delivering a Bible.

Alaina also reportedly told investigators that she woke shortly after midnight on July 15 and found Ahmadzai was not at home. She said she checked his location on her mobile phone.

Ahmadzai was initially arrested on weapons offences before prosecutors charged him with homicide with intent. He also faces allegations of stealing more than €10,000 (around £8,500) from Lisa's bank accounts using her bank cards.

View 4 Images Sharif Ahmadzai was a keen boxer (Image: INSTAGRAM)

Greek authorities say Ahmadzai has admitted moving Lisa's body but denies killing her.

His lawyer, Christos Erdos, confirmed his client did not answer questions during Thursday's hearing.

Following the hearing, a judge ordered Ahmadzai to remain in pre-trial detention while prosecutors continue gathering evidence ahead of future court proceedings. The allegations against Ahmadzai have not been proven in court.

He was later escorted from court by masked police officers and driven away.

Investigators previously said Ahmadzai became a suspect after officers examined CCTV footage recorded close to where Lisa's body was discovered.

View 4 Images Elisabeth Jane Ross was reportedly known to Sharif Ahmadzai through his wife Alaina Hall (Image: Facebook)

Police believe she died several days before she was found, during a period when temperatures in Athens reached 36C. She was formally identified using fingerprint evidence.

Article continues below

Lisa travelled to Greece on June 26 and had initially been staying with friends in the port district of Piraeus.

The Foreign and Commonwealth Office said earlier: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”

A Police Scotland spokesperson previously said: “We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece. Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.”

News.title: Mums and babies risk lives on mega-dinghies in desperate bid to get to UK
News.content:
This is the human face of the Channel boats crisis, desperate people on the final leg of a journey that could kill them.

Our exclusive images show young children, including some in pushchairs, being bussed to board mega-dinghies to get to Britain. Our investigators tracked a group of around 50 migrants, including small children and women earlier this week as they travelled around 40 miles south-west from France’s largest migrant camp at Loon-Plage, near Dunkirk, to Ecault Forest, close to Boulogne.

The group had paid around £1,200 each to make the final leg of their journey to the UK. They also paid extra for lifejackets, sold at stalls in the Loon-Plage camp for up to €50 (£42) – almost double the price in nearby shops.

View 8 Images Katie Sweetingham, head of operations at Care4Calais (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily Express)

‌



English Channel horror as 157 migrants capsize on flaming boat with France and UK launching rescue mission READ MORE :

Three migrants die crossing the Channel after busiest day this year READ MORE :

Katie Sweetingham, Head of Operations at charity Care4Calais, says she has seen increasing numbers of women and children, including babies, at the camp since the UK government indefinitely paused family reunion applications in September last year. She said: “Lots of women and children would use that scheme to be reunited with their loved ones in the UK and now that option is not available. So they have to get into a boat and make that dangerous crossing.”

The journey we saw the migrants make on Thursday seemed complicated. After being taken from the camp to a bus stop in Loon-Plage, the group boarded a bus to Gravelines. Following a lengthy wait, they then took a second bus from Gravelines to Calais, before boarding a train to Boulogne, where they got on another bus to the edge of the forest.

View 8 Images Migrants in Boulogne where they were preparing to take their third bus journey of the day (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily Express)

On getting off the final bus, they made their way along hiking paths to a makeshift dwelling inside the protected natural site, which includes various camping spots for caravans. They appeared to be being guided by a tall man, believed to be Kurdish, who had a distinctive tattoo on his right hand.

‌



French police, including armed gendarmes, followed the migrants throughout the four-hour journey, including walking with them into the forest. But they made no attempt to stop them.

Good weather has led to perfect sailing conditions so far this summer, causing a spike in crossing attempts by gangs. Four migrants, including three women, have died in separate boat tragedies in the Channel in recent days. And with the favourable conditions now expected to continue until at least September, there are fears of more tragedies. Investigators say traffickers are increasingly exploiting the Opal Coast, south of Boulogne, to launch dangerously overloaded rubber boats following a crackdown further north in Calais and Dunkirk.

View 8 Images Stalls, linked to the smuggling gangs, at Loon-Plage migrant camp are selling life jackets for 50 Euros (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily Mirror)

They use new mega-dinghies bought from manufacturers in China. Despite being completely unfit for open seas, the boats are being used to transport more than 150 migrants at a time, netting the gangs up to £200,000 for a single trip. Ordering a mega-dinghy previously took months and involved a 5,500-mile journey by road, via countries including Kazakhstan and Turkey, costing traffickers at least £10,000.

‌



However, we can reveal at least one factory is now offering direct delivery by plane to France, in packages measuring just 2m x 1m x 1m. The vessels are advertised online as Huge Large Super Inflatable Pontoon Rescue Boats, and cost just £1,200. But they are billed as being designed for 40 people, not 150. The maximum delivery time is just two weeks.

View 8 Images Police patrol the beach at Équihen Plage on the lookout for migrants trying to board mega dinghies (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com)

Katie said: “We’ve heard about the bigger dinghies from the people we support. It’s a recent change. It just goes to show that all of the border security measures, largely funded by the UK, don’t do their stated aim of stopping the crossings. All they do is make people that are organising the crossings change their business model, which is now the larger boats, making it much more dangerous for the people that are attempting crossings.”

Katie says she and her team regularly meet children as young as 13 trying to cross to Britain without adult supervision. She said: “It’s usually going to be those younger people that are targeted for driving the boat and then on entry to the UK they’re much more likely to be criminalised and not believed for their age.”

‌



View 8 Images A group of Iraqi Kurdish migrants walk down the main road into Equihen Plage, a popular migrant beach for onward small boat transport to Britain (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com)

A week last Thursday, a boat overturned in the water near Ecault Forest, causing the death of a man and leading to the near-drowning of a baby. The same day, three women in their 20s, 30s and 40s, drowned after an inflatable dinghy with more than 100 people on board capsized near Loon-Plage.

Katie said: “More people are dying trying to make the journey. A lot of them speak to us and say they’ve been on a boat and they’ve seen their friends die in front of them, but then they will say ‘what else can I do?’ There’s no other way for that person to be able to reach safety in the UK to be able to gain asylum other than to repeat that journey again and try again.”

8 View 8 Images Migrants walking down the main road into Equihen Plage on Saturday (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com) 8 View 8 Images Migrants were also seen wandering the many trails inside Écault Forest while waiting for an opportunity to board boats to Britain (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com)

‌



Figures have just revealed the average number of migrants crammed per boat has more than doubled over five years. Analysis found 66 migrants on average have been packed on to each of the 219 vessels to cross the Channel successfully this year. They carried 14,561 passengers in total. An average of 27 per boat was recorded for the whole of 2021, when 1,064 vessels carrying 28,526 migrants made it to the Kent coast.

A source said: “These so-called mega-dinghies are hugely profitable and the smugglers are getting hold of them very easily. Their emergence means a huge number of people can be moved at one time, but always in extremely and increasingly dangerous circumstances. Frankly, it is a nightmare development for the authorities.”

An Egyptian man yesterday began a one-year prison sentence in France after being convicted of trying to smuggle a record 173 migrants into Britain on a 40ft mega-dinghy that burst into flames in the Channel. An Iraqi-born people-smuggler, named by police as Rasoul Halo, was on Tuesday also imprisoned for a year, for smuggling an inflatable boat on to a beach. Halo, who was found with three passports including a British one, claimed he was just helping a friend with a delivery.

News.title: 'Cruel Tory plan to ban non-UK nationals from social housing would see thousands torn out of their homes'
News.content:
'Cruel Tory plan to ban non-UK nationals from social housing would see thousands torn out of their homes'

Writing for the Mirror, Shelter CEO Sarah Elliott slams Tory leader Kemi Badenoch's 'cynical' plans to ban non-UK nationals from social homes - 'it is scapegoating, plain and simple'

View 5 Images Tory plans to ban non-UK nationals from social housing have been slammed (Image: Getty Images)

Another day, another cynical kick-about, where the basic human need for a safe and secure home is punted around like a political football.

‌



Hot on the heels of Reform, who outlined a similar plan earlier this year, the Conservative Party announced on Thursday that it would ban non-UK nationals from social homes in a bid to ‘free up’ a supposed ‘228,144 homes’ for British families and evict existing tenants who aren’t UK or EU nationals.

‌



It goes without saying that this plan is cruel. There are already strict rules on eligibility for social homes, and they are not simply handed out to people on arrival in the UK.

‌



View 5 Images There are already strict rules on eligibility for social homes (Image: Heritage Images via Getty Images)

MI5 and GCHQ chiefs on hunt for young Russian-speaking spies to combat Vladimir Putin threat READ MORE :

Many of the families targeted by this scheme have lived in the country for years or even decades. They settled here and built lives for themselves. They are our friends, neighbours, and colleagues. They work jobs and pay into the system. They are a part of the fabric of our country.

If this plan was rolled out, thousands of people would be torn out of the homes and communities they have spent their whole lives in, with just six months to secure a roof over their heads. Worse still, many will be put at risk of homelessness.

‌



It’s important to remember that those evicted under the scheme will not simply disappear from the system. They will be forced into ludicrously expensive private renting, where rents have soared out of reach of local incomes.

View 5 Images Shelter CEO Sarah Elliott said the proposals were 'cruel' and would worsen the homelessness crisis (Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach Plc)

Social rents cost on average about a third of private rents and, like anyone who sees their rent more than double overnight, many will be forced to rely on housing benefit to make ends meet. Those who can’t afford it will be made homeless. Councils are already shelling out billions every year on the sticking plaster solution of grotty and unstable temporary accommodation.

‌



Announcing the plan, Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary Helen Whately said social homes should not be given out as a ‘free ride on the benefits system’ and that ‘Britain cannot be a cash machine for the world’. But far from saving the taxpayer money, this plan will only serve to pile more costs on to already cash-strapped councils and public services that are stretched to breaking point.

And let’s not forget that social tenants pay rent, which goes back to the public purse and into society. It is completely senseless to ruin people’s lives, drive up homelessness and put extreme pressure on councils for a policy that simply cannot work.

Leaving aside the murky waters the Conservatives could find themselves in if they set about evicting people based on their nationality – a protected characteristic under equality law – let’s call this plan what it is: scapegoating, plain and simple. It’s an attempt by politicians to distract the failures of successive governments, including the Conservative Party, to address the root cause of the housing emergency: our dire shortage of social rent homes.

‌



View 5 Images Shelter runs around 80 charity stores across the UK, alongside an online store (Image: Rutherglen Reformer)

Social rent homes - where rents are pegged to local incomes – are the only genuinely affordable route out of homelessness for struggling families. For years, we have lost more than we’ve built through sales and demolitions and, last year, we only managed to build a measly 12,000 – just 13% of the 90,000 we need every year to end the housing emergency.

When you spell it out, it’s easy to see that the 1.3 million households who are on social housing waiting lists across England are stuck there because of the political failure to build the homes we need, not because of migration. Families who are trapped for months or even years in temporary accommodation are sick of struggling to hold down jobs and settle children in the appalling and insecure conditions they live with every day. But the good news is it doesn’t have to be this way.

‌



There is a clear way for us to ensure everyone has access to a safe, secure and affordable home and that is to build a new generation of social rent homes. Is it possible? Absolutely. Not only that, we have done it before. In 1967, nearly half (46%) of all new homes built in England were for social rent and almost all (97%) were delivered by councils.

View 5 Images Those evicted from social housing under the scheme will not simply disappear from the system, the charity CEO warned (Image: In Pictures via Getty Images)

The Prime Minister hit the nail on the head when he said the solution to the housing emergency is to deliver the ‘biggest council house-building programme since the post-war period’. Councils know their communities better than anyone. They know the kinds of homes local people need, whether it is families looking for a permanent place for their kids to grow up or people rebuilding their lives after spending time on the streets.

Article continues below

Now the government must get on with the job of delivering on the Prime Minister’s vision by helping councils to get spades in the ground and removing the financial barriers that stand in their way.

Migrants didn’t cause the housing emergency, but like many of us, they have suffered the brunt of it. It’s time for politicians of all stripes to stop scoring cheap political points at the expense of their constituents and get on with the job in front of them. Anything else will be a distraction.

News.title: Far-right Clacton by-election candidate 'tried to set off pyrotechnics on pier' as UK battles wildfires
News.content:
Far-right Clacton by-election candidate 'tried to set off pyrotechnics on pier' as UK battles wildfires

By-election candidate Kai Stephens and a group of far-right protesters from the British Democrats attempted to light pyrotechnics on the timber-decked Clacton Pier

Vile remigration banner displayed in Clacton

The owners of Clacton Pier have slammed members of a far-right group who 'tried to set off pyrotechnics' before being forced to leave.

‌



Kai Stephens - a candidate in the upcoming Clacton by-election - was named among the British Democrats group who staged a demonstration without permission at the family attraction today. The men tried to hang a large banner over the side of the pier, the pier's owners said, and held pyrotechnics "with an apparent intention to ignite them".

‌



The group then directed "an unacceptable level of verbal abuse and language" at security guards who asked them to leave, which was branded "wholly inappropriate for a family attraction".

‌



View 3 Images Far-right protesters unfurled the banner after being ejected from Clacton Pier (Image: @LewisNottmPath/x)

Illegal working arrests soar as top Reform figure Zia Yusuf branded 'pillock' over migration plan READ MORE :

One video shared by the British Democrats on social media showed the men unfurling a banner reading 'Save Our Nation - Remigration' on a pedestrian bridge near the pier. Writing on Facebook this afternoon, the owners of Clacton Pier said it "strongly condemns" the protest.

They added: "Bringing pyrotechnics onto the Pier, with an apparent intention to ignite them, was extremely irresponsible, particularly given the prolonged period of dry weather and the Pier’s timber decking. The potential consequences of such actions, including the risk of fire and serious harm to members of the public, are self-evident.

‌



View 3 Images The owners of Clacton Pier said they 'strongly condemned' the protest (Image: Clacton Pier/Facebook)

"Our security team promptly requested that the individuals leave the premises. This request was met with an unacceptable level of verbal abuse and language wholly inappropriate for a family attraction.

"Clacton Pier is a place for everyone, and we firmly believe that visitors should be able to enjoy their day without disruption, intimidation or interference. We will always take appropriate action to protect the safety and enjoyment of our visitors, staff and the Pier itself."

‌



View 3 Images Kai Stephens, 22, is standing for the British Democrats in the Clacton by-election (Image: British Democrats)

Kai Stephens, a 22-year-old far-right activist from Norwich, is one of 34 candidates standing in the Clacton by-election, which is being held on August 13. The by-election was called by Reform UK leader Nigel Farage at an estimated cost of £200,000 to the taxpayer.

Mr Stephen's party, the British Democrats, advocates "voluntary repatriation" and "remigration" of immigrants in a bid to stave off what it claims is the "demographic replacement" of the British people. He told the Eastern Daily Press this week that Farage was his "political hero from a young age", but that he now believes his "weak policies on immigration would do nothing to prevent Britain's decline".

Article continues below

Mr Stephens stood for the party in the Norwich City Council local elections back in May, finishing last of six candidates in the Crome ward, with 77 votes. The Mirror has contacted the British Democrats for comment.

News.title: Andy Burnham to embark on cost of living tour through the UK
News.content:
The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.

No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.

But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales â with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.

Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living â although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.

Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles â like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off â must be accepted as part of life.

"He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."

The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are.

"The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."

There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.

One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.

But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme â including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.

The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.

But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.

The Conservatives said the government's "tax hikes and red tape are hammering our high streets".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride said: "This is breathtaking hypocrisy from Burnhamâ¦ they are forcing businesses to close, destroying jobs and driving up prices for the public.

"Meanwhile, Labour are plotting to release dangerous criminals onto our streets, leaving people feeling unsafe in their communities."

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper said struggling high street businesses "need more than a new PM embarking on a vanity tour this summer".

She said the PM should adopt the Lib Dem plan for high streets: "That means reversing the damaging jobs tax, delivering an emergency VAT cut for hospitality, replacing broken business rates and cracking down on the ghost landlords leaving our shop fronts vacant."

Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "If Andy Burnham wants to help people with the cost of living, he should scrap the green levies and taxes on energy bills and rule out tax rises at the Budget."

News.title: Fifa criticises campaign to oust president Infantino
News.content:
Fifa has strongly criticised what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and its president Gianni Infantino.

The statement follows a Daily Telegraph report, external which claimed Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment by Uefa after he had an affair while he was its general secretary.

A Fifa spokesperson told the Telegraph Infantino "strongly denies" the allegations and that they are "categorically untrue".

Fifa has now itself hit out at "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims", adding that "speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact".

Infantino has come under increasing pressure from Uefa and European football associations over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

Uefa has said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness on Friday called on the Swiss-Italian to resign.

European football's governing body says its threat to boycott Fifa events remains on the table, adding that assurances the FFE plan could not be revived have not been received.

"The Fifa president was democratically elected by Fifa's Member Associations and continues to serve with their mandate," Fifa said in its statement on Saturday.

"It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president.

"Those who do not have the support of Fifa's member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa's established democratic processes."

Opposition to Infantino is largely from within Europe.

The Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.

It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa member countries.

Infantino is also unanimously backed by the 54 nations of the Confederation of African Football (Caf).

News.title: Killed a month after his wedding - why PC Andrew Harper's death touched so many
News.content:
On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.

Instead, it was uniformed officers, there to tell her that the man she had married four weeks earlier had been killed while on police duty.

"Everything I had known in my life to be true was robbed away. Every ounce of beautiful peace, gone," Lissie later said of the moment she was told.

They had met as teenagers and were together for 13 years.

In her eulogy at his funeral, Lissie recalled how Andrew would pass her notes in class.

They were, she said, "true childhood sweethearts, loving one another more and more with each passing day".

They had been about to go on their honeymoon.

But, on that night nearly seven years ago, everything changed.

The case has been back in the headlines because two of PC Harper's killers â Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole â will become eligible to be released early under government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.

As the disturbing details of the case are revisited, his family, fellow officers and the public are outraged once more â at what happened, and at the perpetrators' impending release.

PC Harper's death was brutal and devastating, causing shock, anger and an outpouring of grief across the country.

Pictures of the smiling faces of his teenage killers laughing and joking as they left court only added to that anger.

PC Harper had been about to head home at the end of a long shift when he and a colleague were called to reports of a burglary.

He was "going beyond the call of duty", the prosecutor at the Old Bailey trial in 2020 said.

During the case, haunting dashcam footage from the police patrol car was played showing the moment PC Harper confronted teenagers Henry Long, Bowers and Cole down a dark country lane. He then disappeared from view.

His ankles had got caught in a strap trailing behind the car being driven by Long that had been used to tow a stolen quad bike.

PC Harper was dragged for over a mile. He died on the road. His police badge and stab vest were found scattered along the route.

The three teenagers were tried for murder. In the end, the jury convicted Bowers and Cole of manslaughter. Long had already pleaded guilty to that offence.

It meant the jury was not sure that PC Harper's killers knew they were dragging the officer behind the car.

But the Judge, Mr Justice Edis, described it as a manslaughter case which was "very close to a case of murder" in its seriousness.

News.title: Israel accused of weaponising archaeology at ancient West Bank sites
News.content:
Up in the hills above the Roman columns of the ancient site of Sebastia, in the occupied West Bank, are olive fields that have been cultivated for generations by Palestinian families.

One of the landowners, Abu Mudif, says he has received notification that his land is part of a tranche of about 450 acres that the Israeli authorities are taking possession of in order, they say, to protect and develop the site for a major new national park.

Typically, Palestinian landowners receive little or no payment for such land expropriation. And even when it is offered, most refuse it as they see accepting it as giving recognition and legitimacy to the loss of what they see as their patrimony.

It's a vital income for Abu Mudif to lose of course, but it goes deeper than that for him.

News.title: Australia is the planet's extinction hotspot, but one animal offers a glimmer of hope
News.content:
"Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat.

Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement.

Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater.

Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland â in the south-western corner of Australia â is one of the few places they remain.

As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival.

Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency.

This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change.

Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion.

News.title: Kellie Bright to leave EastEnders after 13 years
News.content:
EastEnders star Kellie Bright is to leave the soap after playing one of its key characters, Linda Carter, for 13 years.

She arrived in Albert Square with on-screen husband Mick, portrayed by Danny Dyer, when they became the new owners of the Queen Vic pub.

Carter's matriarch character has been central to major storylines including plots about murder, sexual assault and alcoholism.

Bright said she made the "tough decision" to leave more than a year ago but "happily" agreed to stay on to be part of an "exciting storyline".

The BBC has promised "unmissable drama" before her on-screen exit, which is said to be a "while away" yet.

Executive producer Ben Wadey described the actor as being "the beating heart of EastEnders" and said she had become "a classic EastEnders icon".

Viewers have seen the much-loved character at the heart of many emotional storylines including in 2014 when she was raped by her brother-in-law Dean Wicks.

More than 7m people watched the episode which prompted dozens of complaints. The sexual assualt led to long-running story arc about family conflict and trauma.

News.title: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock
News.content:
"I can't zip this! Mummm?"

This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.

The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.

She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood.

"She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me.

"It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off."

"Iâm still in shock,â she adds. âThe thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."

The interaction went viral, external with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.

While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" â where stars match outfits to a film's themes â Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.

Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun.

"Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.â

News.title: How weight-loss medication is changing relationships with alcohol
News.content:
There is a growing body of research into the link between weight-loss drugs and alcohol consumption.

The drugs, with brands including Wegovy, Mounjaro and Ozempic, contain semaglutide or tirzepatide, which mimic a natural hormone called GLP-1. This suppresses appetite and keeps people feeling fuller for longer, helping them to lose weight.

Early research suggests that because these drugs affect the reward response in the brain, they can reduce cravings for substances including alcohol and nicotine, says Dr Christian Hendershot of the University of South Carolina.

He published a small-scale study, external in 2025 in which participants with alcohol use disorder craved alcohol less while taking Ozempic. Alcohol use disorder, sometimes referred to as alcoholism, is described by the NHS as drinking in a way that is harmful.

A study, external from the University of Colorado Anschutz published last week also suggested that GLP-1 medications in pill form led to fewer days of heavy drinking in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder.

People taking the drugs told BBC News that alcohol had affected them in different ways: some said their cravings for it had gone, drinking had made them feel nauseous or uncomfortably full, or they had got drunk more quickly. Others said they had not noticed any effect on their relationship with alcohol.

Before she started taking Wegovy, Lisa says she drank between six and eight bottles of wine a week with friends. But she had sometimes worried about whether this was too much and whether it could damage her health.

NHS guidance, external is that people should not drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, which is about six medium glasses of wine or six pints. Drinking too much in the long term can lead to liver damage, high blood pressure and increased risk of cancer.

Lisa says that since starting on the medication she has more than halved her consumption. At a recent day festival, she drank three glasses of wine over the course of nine hours. Previously, she would have had two bottles plus a couple of vodka mixers, she says.

Alcohol has always been a big part of her social life and when she stopped drinking for a few weeks in the late 2010s, she realised friends had stopped inviting her to social events. It led her to start drinking again.

This time round, Lisa says that she still looks forward to drinking wine, but after having a couple of glasses she simply cannot stomach any more.

"I still feel involved in things because I'm still drinking but drinking a lot less," Lisa says.

For years, Warren Thomas, 45, from Colchester, had enjoyed an occasional beer with his family after work, as well as one or two heavy drinking sessions with his friends each month.

But when he spoke to his friends on weight-loss medication about his plans to start taking Mounjaro, they warned him that it could affect how much he drank.

Warren says he noticed the effect within 24 hours of his first dose in mid-June. "I just don't want to drink," he says. "I've just got no appetite for it."

When he went out for his friend's birthday last month, he felt "light-headed and a little bit giddy" after two beers, he says.

"My tolerance level to drinking is now zero," he says.

There is no formal advice in the British National Formulary, a guide to dispensing medicine used by doctors and pharmacists, about whether people on weight-loss drugs should stop drinking alcohol, says Prof Russell Hearn, a GP and professor of medicine at King's College London.

But he gives careful advice to his patients. "Alcohol has a lot of calories in it and if your goal is to lose weight, drinking less will definitely help you with that alongside changing your diet while you're on a GLP-1," he says.

For people like Lisa and Warren, drinking less alcohol has been a happy bonus. But recent graduate Faye Goodwin, 20, feels that it has hampered her social life.

When Faye drinks she says she gets nauseous very quickly and sometimes throws up or gets bad acid reflux.

Faye, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice, has been taking Mounjaro since she was 18 and does not really know what it is like to drink alcohol without the impact of weight-loss medication. But she says she once took a month off the jabs and was able to drink without experiencing any nausea.

News.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
News.content:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost Â£150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than Â£85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent Â£50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further Â£35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

News.title: Simon Levy victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures'
News.content:
Police have urged more victims of Simon Levy to come forward, as London's victims' commissioner said a "litany of failures" had allowed him to kill two women and rape a third.

Andrea Simon called for a review on the "failure to monitor him appropriately" when the 40-year-old was known to police as a sexual predator.

British Transport Police said women who recognised Levy as their attacker should report it, while the Met Police said it had investigated whether he had more victims, including further murders.

Meanwhile, the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) said a police constable is under investigation for gross misconduct, and a detective sergeant is facing a misconduct investigation.

On Friday, Levy was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London while he was being monitored by the Met Police for being a convicted sex offender. He had previously committed a string of sex attacks.

The BBC reported how a series of grave failings by police, prosecutors and the courts left Levy free to murder, rape and sexually assault women.

Levy is due to be sentenced on Wednesday.

News.title: Widdecombe police reopen investigation into incident at Farage's home, BBC understands
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the killing of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident at Nigel Farage's south London home, the BBC understands.

It is understood to relate to what the Reform UK leader described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said it was looking into an "attempted burglary" at a property as part of the Widdecombe murder investigation, but did not confirm the home was linked to Farage or why it might be connected to the killing of the former MP.

CTP London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation into the Farage incident was handled.

Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".

A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."

CTP London said it would "full engage" with the watchdog's investigation, adding: "The victims and families in both investigations have been updated today, and we continue to support them."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Woman attacked by bed bugs during Travelodge stay
News.content:
Thirteen days after Hannah Stephenson stayed a night in a Travelodge hotel, she is still itching with red lumps over her body - a nightmare she would not wish on her "worst enemy".

The 31-year-old from Bassingbourn had been out with friends in Cambridge and decided to book a one-night stay at the hotel on Newmarket Road on 26 July to save money instead of getting a taxi home.

The next morning, she woke up to a "horrible realisation", feeling itchy with red lumps over her body and blood spots smeared on the bedding â the tell-tale signs of bed bugs, she said.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and how distressing an incident like this can be."
