World.title: Planes in tarmac near miss at Sydney Airport
World.content:
The ABC understands a Jetstar plane has been involved in a near miss with a Qatar Airlines plane on the tarmac at Sydney Airport this morning.

A Jetstar cabin crew worker was injured and assessed by paramedics. No passengers were injured.

It is understood the Jetstar plane had to brake suddenly to avoid a collision about 7am.

The Gold Coast-bound flight was taxiing to the runway when the incident occurred.

The ABC understands air traffic control was under operating restrictions from 6am to 8am this morning, reducing the number of planes flying in and out of the airport.

"Our aircraft was following instructions by Air Traffic Control when the pilots were forced to brake firmly after another aircraft came in close proximity," a Jetstar spokesperson said.

"We have commenced an investigation into the incident."

It comes after Airservices Australia on Saturday said it was "working to address rostering issues" amid delays on the runway for multiple days in a row.

More than 150 flights were impacted as a result of roster constraints affecting the airport.

World.title: Portrait of domestic life wins $40,000 photography prize
World.content:
Paul Knight, an artist from Ettalong Beach in New South Wales, has won the National Photography Prize from the Murray Art Museum Albury (MAMA).

It is Australia's longest-running acquisitive photographic award and offers the $40,000 Audray Banfield Award.





The Chamber Music series documents the life Paul Knight shares with his partner, Peter. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Allison Jess) Knight's winning series of work, titled Chamber Music, documents the domestic life he shares with his partner, Peter, and the way relationships are shaped every day.

Knight was one of the 12 finalists for the prize, alongside Alana Hunt, Alex Walker, Amalia Lindo, Arlo Mountford, David Stephenson, JD Reforma, Lisa Stonham, Marian Tubbs, Morgan Hogg, Nathanael Edwards, and Sarah Rhodes.

Works of the finalists can now be seen in the 2026 National Photography Prize exhibition.

The announcement was made at Saturday's opening of the event, where Morgan Hogg was also awarded the $5,000 Emerging Artist Award for their work Silver Tongues, exploring the mythology and storytelling of the Pacific.

Morgan Hogg won the $5,000 John and Margaret Baker Fellowship. (Supplied: MAMA Albury )

Through a traditional Cook Island dance, Hogg explores the role of the Momokē, the water people of the underworld, who lure the souls of those who are almost ready to move onto the next life.

More than 330 artists entered this year's competition, with a curatorial committee comprising MAMA CEO Blair French, 2024 National Photography Prize recipient Ellen Dahl, and MAMA First Nations Curator Alinta Maguire selecting the 12 finalists.

Part of Alana Hunt's work included 64 polaroids. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Allison Jess)

National Gallery of Victoria senior curator of photography Natasha Bullock selected the winner of the National Photography Prize and the Emerging Artist Award.

“The work really captures the freedom with which artists are working today," Ms Bullock said. "Photography can be intimate, it can be highly conceptual or technically experimental and it can embrace all of the above. What’s exciting is the way these finalists are bringing all of these possibilities together, and finding new ways to make us look and see."

The Hear No, See No, Speak No series by Nathanael Edwards. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Allison Jess)

Mr French said this year's finalists were from Far North Queensland, Tasmania, regional NSW, Sydney and Melbourne and had varied levels of experience, from early career to "40-plus years" in the industry.

"The work is diverse and covers many themes and concepts, including family history, intimate stories, memories, environment, cultural identity, and connections to place," said Mr French.

Mr French says MAMA has a reputation for having a significant photography collection. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Allison Jess)

Mr French said the biennial competition is unique, as it looks at a collection of the artist's work, created in the past two years, rather than just one piece.

"You have a range of works by an artist that give you pause to consider and that's pretty rare in art prizes," he said.

The powerhouse behind the prize

The National Photography Prize was first held by MAMA, then known as the Albury Regional Art Gallery, in 1983.

The idea came from the inaugural director of the gallery, the late Audray Banfield.

A 2004 portrait of the late Audray Banfield, who was a well-known advocate for photography. (Supplied: Jules Boag and Rita Lazauskas, MAMA Collection)

Over the years, Ms Banfield helped to build the museum's growing collection of contemporary photography, which today includes more than 600 works, including important pieces by Tracey Moffatt, Max Dupain, Richard Woldendorp and Phillip Quirk.

Mr French said Ms Banfield's name has officially been attached to the $40,000 award this year.

"The gallery was founded and opened in 1981, and that's when Audray decided to make photography a focus of the gallery, with an aim to build on a collection of national significance," he said.

"When Audray passed away in 2024, we found it was appropriate to honour her within the museum and within the photography community."

The $40,000 is funded by the MAMA Art Foundation, which is an entity separate to the museum and focused on fundraising and advocating for the museum and its collection.

The Albury Regional Art Gallery was officially renamed the Murray Art Museum Albury after renovations in 2015. (ABC Goulburn Murray: Allison Jess)

This year the award for the National Photography Prize was increased from $30,000 to $40,000.

"When we sat down with the foundation and talked about naming the main award after Audray, we also asked them to think about lifting the prize amount," Mr French said.

"It has sat at $30,000 for a while and the way the world is, to put a little bit more money into artists pockets is an important part of what we are trying to do."

The National Photography Prize exhibition is at MAMA until November 22.

World.title: Perez Hilton in serious but stable condition following self-harm incident
World.content:
Graphic content CultureCelebrityMental health Perez Hilton in serious but stable condition following self-harm incident Nell Geraets August 9, 2026 — 11:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Perez Hilton is in “serious but stable condition” and will require surgery after he appeared to commit self-harm in a livestream earlier this week, according to a new statement written by his family. “He experienced significant blood loss and sustained additional injuries that will require surgery in the coming days,” Hilton’s family wrote on his website PerezHilton.com on Sunday. “His treatment and recovery will be a long process. We are grateful that Perez was able to spend time with his mother and sister yesterday.” Perez Hilton remains in hospital where he will undergo surgery in the coming days. Getty The celebrity blogger was hospitalised on August 4 after sharing a TikTok livestream in which he appeared to harm himself. Concerned viewers notified the authorities, which prompted a police response. Hilton was then hospitalised under Florida’s Baker Act – a law allowing authorities to involuntarily hold someone for a period of time if they pose a threat of harm to themselves or others. The family’s statement demanded privacy, urging members of both the media and public to stop visiting Hilton’s property.



“There is absolutely no reason for members of the media or the public to remain outside the family’s home,” the statement read. “We again respectfully ask members of the media to leave the home and surrounding area, stop following family members, and cease photographing Perez’s children. We also ask photo agencies not to purchase, publish, or distribute any photographs of the children that may have been taken.” Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s deputies visited the home where Perez Hilton was found after he appeared to harm himself during a TikTok livestream. Getty Images According to the statement, Hilton’s three children (whom he had via surrogacy) remain safe and are being cared for by immediate family. “Please allow them, and the rest of the family, the peace and privacy they desperately need during this incredibly difficult time. Thank you for your continued support, compassion and understanding.” In an earlier update, Hilton’s family said the blogger was able “to communicate”, which gave them hope.



Related Article Graphic content

Mental health Perez Hilton’s children ‘fled’ home minutes before ‘severe mental health crisis’ Since then, however, they said there had been several “false and inaccurate” reports regarding the blogger’s condition. “We want to confirm that Perez remains hospitalised under Florida’s Baker Act. His communication has been extremely limited and confined to immediate family, medical providers and others directly involved in his care.” There has been no communication between Hilton and the media, the statement continued, and he has not issued any public statements. “The only statements regarding Perez that should be considered credible and authorised are those published directly on PerezHilton.com.” On August 6, the family revealed in a separate statement that Hilton’s children and other family members had been inside the home on August 4, just minutes before the livestream began. They reportedly fled the property once it became clear he was experiencing a severe mental health crisis.



Authorities from the Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office attended the 48-year-old blogger’s home after receiving several calls from concerned members of the public who had seen a distressing livestream of Hilton appearing to harm himself. Hilton’s TikTok account has since been suspended. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636. World.title: Religion is no reason to hate
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The story in the Sun-Herald about the help given by Rahemath Pasha to victims during the Bondi tragedy was inspirational (“This Indian Uber driver helped save lives at Bondi. Now he’s able to call Sydney home”, August 2). To quote him: “No religion will teach you to harm anyone.” Also, he states, “I have been taught from my religion [to] always help people.” He is a Muslim from the same city in India as the accused gunman. It just goes to show how every group can have good or bad among it and makes nonsense of any proposed policy to limit immigrant groups of a certain religion or ethnicity. Ruth Carter, Strathfield Rahemath Pasha was diagnosed with PTSD after helping multiple victims of the Bondi shootings. He has been granted permanent residence in Australia. Janie Barrett Learning, not earning Here’s a better solution to fixing the school system, Helen Lewin (Letters, August 2). It’s also the way one of the world’s most successful education systems does things. Finland strictly regulates it education model and does not permit mainstream schools to operate for profit or charge tuition fees. While its educational performance went from low to high under this system, Australia’s went from high to low under our increasingly privatised system. If we followed Finland’s example, all that private money inefficiently spent on private schools could be invested in building new housing. David McMaster, Mosman Productivity a priority We are fortunate that Parnell Palme McGuinness will never have a voice in the economic management of Australia. Her article on the difficult issues of balancing possible wage increases or price decreases does not mention productivity once (“Quick-fix schemes will ruin the nation”, August 2), yet it is a key problem for Australia and has been stuck for some decades, as shown in the Productivity Commission’s figures since 1978. To invent new conspiracy theory terms like “wage fakery” will not cut it as any kind of quick fix. Bill Johnstone, Blackheath



A work in progress Jacqueline Maley makes some great points about fraught gender roles, but the real elephant in the room is capitalism (“Why the tradwife trend is totally logical” August 2). After World War II, as growth in manufacturing led to more jobs that often required higher literacy and cognitive skills, women were drafted into the workforce in large numbers to work alongside men. It was the realisation that most jobs could be done by either sex, coupled with women’s new financial empowerment and the availability of reliable contraception that really turbo-charged feminism. But the ensuing rise in each household’s financial capacity led to a rapid rise in house prices, locking both women and men into the workforce and forcing young children into brokered care. Today, employers unwilling to keep salaries commensurate with the cost of living are looking to AI to exploit ever cheaper and faster sources of labour to chase profits that only robotic slaves can possibly deliver. Vivienne Peters, Hornsby At 57, I am a woman of yesteryear. Instead of tradwifery, I was raised a Catholic. Be warned young women and men, whoever you let hold the power over you, even inadvertently, the script can change whenever they choose. And you will realise those that held the power over you were never living the life they proclaimed because it is a fallacy. The message of religious conformity is simply about control and until you realise that you will surrender your precious opportunity for autonomy instead of realising that the true gift of life is to believe in yourself. Jenny Stephenson, Wollongong Taken for granted Your correspondent wonders what would be left in the British Museum if “stuff the British stole” was returned to its rightful owners (Letters, August 2). For a bit of balance I look forward to a similar inquiry into the other colonial powers that also had considerably sticky fingers: France, Belgium, Holland, Spain, Germany, Italy, Portugal and even Japan, Russia and the US – but they seem to get off scot-free. I wonder why? Judy Hungerford, Narraweena Study in contrast Study, work and public space has definitely changed since my youth (“Old bookstore turns a page as a ‘Hogwarts’ study space”, August 2). It is exciting to see the changes within Sydney accommodating young people, surrounded by used books, Hogwarts and Ghibli paraphernalia, what better way to inspire, or relax, or at least reduce anxiety in a study/work day? Fortunately, our local library in Thirroul attempts to create a similar environment, where silence is definitely no longer a requirement. It, too, is vibrant, accommodating and welcoming for all ages and interest groups. The librarians are also on hand to help. It is fabulous to see families and friends, not just visiting and borrowing, but spending quality time together and feeling so at home in their local library. Janice Creenaune, Austinmer

World.title: In confirming Blanche as US A-G, senators endorse a Justice Department under Trump’s sway
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS politics In confirming Blanche as US A-G, senators endorse a Justice Department under Trump’s sway Glenn Thrush August 9, 2026 — 10:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The three lame-duck Republican senators who narrowly saved Todd Blanche’s confirmation as US attorney-general ended up backing him because they believed he was the only person who had earned enough trust, and enjoyed enough access, to rein in President Donald Trump. One issue with that calculation: Blanche is a champion of unbridled presidential power. Time and again during his turbulent nomination process, Blanche made it unmistakably clear that he believes Trump possesses a nearly limitless right to directly control the actions of the Justice Department under Article II of the Constitution. It is an argument that formed the foundation of his strategy as the president’s criminal defence lawyer and is the lodestar of his government service. Todd Blanche has sidestepped questions over whether actions Donald Trump ordered were right, saying only that Trump had the right to do them. Bloomberg Blanche’s confirmation in the predawn hours of Saturday (Washington time) was largely symbolic: as acting attorney general, he could have served indefinitely. But it represented a powerful endorsement by Congress of the philosophy that has guided him under a meddling, demanding boss – that he has a constitutional obligation to execute every lawful White House order, even if it shatters long-standing policy and rule-of-law norms, or contradicts what he thinks is right.



He articulated that view from the moment he took over as acting attorney-general in April, telling reporters that Trump had “the right” and “duty” to order up investigations of people he targets. During his confirmation, both in public and in private conversations, Blanche sidestepped questions over whether actions Trump ordered were right, saying only that Trump had the right to do them. Related Article Trump's White House ‘Get-out-of-jail-free card’: Trump lawsuit deal bars tax probes against him or his family – forever Barbara McQuade, a University of Michigan Law School professor and former federal prosecutor, said this marked a major break from past administrations. “Just because a president can control the Justice Department does not mean he should,” she said. “Since Watergate, America has prized a Justice Department that is independent from partisan politics.” While Trump and allies such as Blanche have repeatedly accused the Biden White House of ordering up prosecutorial hit jobs against Republicans, they have provided little evidence to support the kind of direct interventions that have become commonplace in Trump’s second term. In a recent interview, former president Barack Obama said he followed a broad rule of remaining at a distance from the Justice Department to protect its independence, even though he was not legally required to do so.



“The White House shouldn’t be able to direct the attorney-general to go around prosecuting whoever the president wants to prosecute,” he said. “The idea is that the attorney-general is the people’s lawyer. It’s not the president’s consiglieri.” Trump has a different view. Case in point: late on Monday, he browbeat US Attorney Jeanine Pirro for withdrawing the indictment of a man accused of defacing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. While the melodramatic showdown was big news, the fact that the president was issuing marching orders to a federal prosecutor was so typical under this administration that it was not noted in most of the coverage. Trump had threatened to temporarily withdraw Blanche’s nomination until two lawmakers who opposed it were out of office. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson During Blanche’s confirmation hearing, Democratic senator Chris Coons asked whether the department he was running is “independent from the White House?” Blanche’s reply: “Article II of the Constitution gives the power of the executive to President Trump.”



When Coons followed up by asking if he would resign if Trump directed him to do something illegal or unethical, Blanche said: “That will never happen. But yes, if it were to happen, I’m not going to violate my oath to the Constitution.” While many Republicans raised questions about Blanche’s actions and even his independence during his confirmation, few were willing to withhold, or even leverage, their votes to challenge the boss-employee dynamic Trump has imposed on the department. Bill Cassidy announced on Friday that he would deliver the decisive vote for Blanche’s confirmation. AP Photo/Rod Lamkey “Ultimately, decisions are made by the president,” said Republican senator Bill Cassidy, who announced in a floor speech on Friday that he would deliver the decisive vote for Blanche’s confirmation. The adviser Cassidy consulted before making up his mind was notable. During his speech, he quoted extensively from conversations with William Barr, Trump’s attorney-general in his first term who articulated an expansive view of presidential power in a 2018 memo. Barr quit two years later when pressured by Trump to help undermine confidence in the 2020 election.



Barr counselled Cassidy to support Blanche in the belief that he could quietly talk the president out of bad ideas, even though Barr quit rather than comply with Trump’s demands to investigate an election Barr found had been fairly conducted. Related Article Trump's White House Inside the showdown that saved a Trump true believer her job Blanche’s experience as Trump’s private lawyer was not a reason to oppose him, Barr told Cassidy – but an asset. It gave Blanche the capacity to “have tough conversations” and confront Trump with “difficult truths” that could change his mind, Barr said to him. Not every Republican bought in to this job description of an attorney-general. Two Republican women, senators Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowksi of Alaska, said they would vote no on Blanche precisely because he had been unwilling to speak truth to Trump’s power or have enough tough conversations with him.



Collins, the first Republican to oppose Blanche, said he had taken several actions “that have further eroded the department’s independence”, including his sign-off on tax protections for the president and his family and the attempted indictments of Democratic lawmakers who criticised Trump. Related Article Analysis

Trump's America Pool fiasco reflects poorly on the morals of an entire administration Early on Friday, Murkowski, a consistent and plainspoken Republican critic of Trump, described her no vote as a moment of major historic consequence – an opportunity to both demonstrate the chamber’s dissatisfaction with Blanche’s obeisance and reclaim the Senate’s authority to influence the department’s direction. “The country needs an attorney-general who will check the worst impulses of this administration,” Murkowski said on Friday. “I hope Mr Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case.” Shortly after, Cassidy took to the floor to offer Blanche his support.



The floor fight over Blanche was preceded by a clash in the Senate Judiciary Committee that followed a similar trajectory. Two lame-duck senators, Republicans John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, briefly withheld their support on the Senate judiciary committee over Blanche’s role in a deal to resolve Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS. The ensuing agreement created a $US1.8 billion ($2.5 billion) fund to compensate purported victims of Biden-era abuses at the department and granted Trump sweeping immunity from tax investigations. Both made it clear, from the start, that they liked Blanche and did not consider his reluctance to challenge Trump to be disqualifying. They simply wanted him to put in writing his verbal commitment to kill the fund and to include modest limits on the tax provision. Blanche was amenable, but the White House resisted, and Trump threatened to temporarily withdraw Blanche’s nomination until the two lawmakers were out of office. The president eventually relented, clearing the way for a vote on the floor. But the episode underscored, in the view of critics, the lopsided power dynamic inherent in the partnership between Trump and Blanche.

World.title: Win City2Surf, turn around, run 14km back: a champion’s Sunday schedule
World.content:
PoliticsNSWCity to Surf Win City2Surf, turn around, run 14km back: a champion’s Sunday schedule Patrick Begley August 9, 2026 — 9:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After tasting victory in this year’s 14-kilometre City2Surf race, Andy Buchanan said he planned to change shoes and “run back to the start”. He has marathons to train for, after all. The 35-year-old Victorian, who held the Australian marathon record, crossed the line first in a field of about 90,000 participants, with a time of 40 minutes and 27 seconds. The course record of 40:03, set by Olympian Steve Moneghetti in 1991, grew a year older.



“I missed it by a fair bit this year, but I’ll be back to try to get it,” said Buchanan, who represented Australia in the marathon at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham. More than 90,000 people are taking part in this year’s City2Surf. Oscar Colman Related Article City to Surf Meet the Babblers: The City2Surf’s most talkative squad Holly Campbell took out the women’s race, crossing the line at Bondi in 46:35. Competing in the elite category of the race for the first time, the 30-year-old surpassed the time her twin sister Paige set when she came second two years ago. “I dreamed about winning this race as a kid,” Campbell, who grew up on a farm in central NSW, said. “Dreams do come true.”



Not everyone was taking the world’s biggest fun run so seriously. A group of four runners dressed as football referees and linesmen were “just keeping everyone in check”, with a whistle and a red card in the pocket. Not chickening out: City2Surf participants making their way towards Bondi. Oscar Colman Many more wore costumes, for a laugh or for charity. Participants have raised more than $63 million for good causes since the fundraising total was first recorded in 2008. The race began at 7.30am, but before dawn contestants had begun to gather at the start line near Hyde Park in the CBD.



Diego Soto, wearing blue-tinted aviator sunglasses, was hoping for a time below an hour. His strategy was “run fast before Heartbreak Hill”, the steep stretch between Rose Bay and Vaucluse. Another early riser, Dan Agnew, said “everybody complains about it” but he liked Heartbreak Hill. “It’s actually really cool,” said Agnew, who was also hoping for a sub-60 minute time. Jessy Bonney’s pre-race preparation included listening to “upbeat emo music” as she readied herself to draw on the crowd’s momentum. “You feel everybody’s energy for the ‘ready, set, go’, you just use it,” Bonney said. “You’re part of that bubble.” Omid Toloo said he has run the race since 1996. Oscar Colman



Personal trainer Omid Toloo said this year’s City2Surf would be his 31st and he hoped there would be many more to come. “If I last until I’m 80, I’m happy.” The Morning Edition newsletter is our guide to the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up here.

World.title: Two planes involved in near-miss while taxiing at Sydney Airport
World.content:
Two planes have been involved in a near-miss while taxiing on the runway at Sydney Airport, forcing one plane to brake suddenly and injuring a crew member.

A Qatar Airways plane and a Jetstar plane were photographed on the runway metres from each other just after 7am on Sunday.

A Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways plane on the runway at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning. Nine News

There were 180 passengers on board Jetstar flight JQ402, which was heading to the Gold Coast, when the pilot spotted a Qatar Boeing 777 aircraft next to the plane, Nine News reported. The Qatar plane did not have any passengers on board and was being towed at the time, according to the report.

The pilot applied the brakes on the Airbus A320, causing one flight attendant who was moving throughout the cabin to fall. The attendant was treated by paramedics for minor injuries. No passengers were injured.

World.title: Skinny is the new skinny: how body extremes reflect the zeitgeist
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSocial media Opinion Skinny is the new skinny: how body extremes reflect the zeitgeist Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist August 9, 2026 — 9:30am

August 9, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has proven himself incapable, so far, of winning the unnecessary Iran war he started with his president, Donald Trump. So when he announced last month that he was going to be testing all “war fighters” in the US military for their testosterone levels, it was tempting to believe Hegseth was projecting, to use the psychological term for when someone attributes their own weaknesses to another person. Ariana Grande’s video for her song Petal has led to comments about her weight. YouTube “Under the supervision of our world-class medical professionals, war fighters age 30 and older are going to be tested annually as part of their periodic health assessment,” Hegseth said in a video posted to X, titled “The High-T Department of War”. Addressing his troops, but only the male ones, it seems, he said the military needs to “constantly look for new ways to optimise your performance … ensuring you have the right testosterone levels to operate at your absolute best”.



He said troops with low testosterone levels would be topped up with hormone replacement therapy, to restore their “natural” function. I’m no expert in military strategy, but even setting aside what such a pronouncement might do for the morale of your personnel, it seems strange to signal to your enemies that your troops might not be man enough. It also sends a strong exclusionary signal to all women in the US military, from the same man who has blocked the recommended promotions of high-ranking women and people of colour, to a disproportionate degree. As the United States polarises ever further politically, it seems the extremism in politics is jumping the fence and moving into other areas of public life – notably gender politics and the way men and women present themselves physically. As men are encouraged to looksmaxx and take peptides to get larger and more imposing, to drive their muscles into hard edges and plane their chins to strong, manly angles, women are shrinking.



The extreme of the late-noughties body positivity movement, where some unhealthy bodies were presented as celebratory and desirable, has now swung to the other end of the pendulum. “Clavicular” is the physical ideal of young men who are “looksmaxxing”. Aresna Villanueva A new kind of (possibly peptide-charged) thinness is now normal and increasingly common. We see it on red carpets and in movies and on all the celebrity Instagram accounts, usually attributed to a Pilates regime and plenty of green juice. This week, the pop star Ariana Grande drew widespread attention when she released a music video for her new song “Petal” in which she looks skeletal, the bones of her shoulders protruding like those of a famine-struck child.



Grande has shrunk herself into cartoonishly tiny proportions, and yet, the narrative of the film clip depicts a jobbing actress being repeatedly rejected by a panel of ugly studio-exec men for being “not good enough”. The video ends with Grande, in character, returning to the audition room with a chainsaw and hacking the men to bloody pieces. One minute she is cloyingly seeking their approval, the next she is massacring them: talk about extremes. Fans have taken to social media to express concern about Grande’s gaunt appearance, and it has sparked multiple think-pieces on Substack and in major newspapers about whether it’s okay to comment on women’s bodies, even when it’s under the guise of worrying about their health. Grande has this week released a statement saying she will be “taking a step back from visibility”.



It is perhaps a small consolation that men now subject themselves to this sort of body scrutiny, and they are subjected to it in the media, too. This week The Times of London published an article about the “mini-paunch” of newly anointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The article noted that Burnham is “slim and fit” and has competed in various marathons. But “despite his efforts the new PM has found attention directed to his barely there mini-paunch, somewhat unfairly dubbed the ‘Burnham belly’”. But the tone of the article was interesting – rather than fat-shaming Burnham, his problem paunch was framed as something that can happen to even the healthiest of men, and nothing terribly serious to worry about.



Related Article Opinion

Eating disorders Is it OK to mention how skinny female celebrities are getting? Again? Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist The writer shared various tips to get rid of male belly fat, if you really wanted to. By contrast, Burnham’s wife, Marie-France Van Heel, was widely critiqued online for wearing a baby blue Victoria Beckham midi-dress on her first official outing with her husband. I thought she looked great, but internet trolls did what they do to women who aren’t within the boundaries of whatever they decree is acceptable. The casual fat-shaming of a prime ministerial wife and the skinny-shaming of a famous pop star are probably two sides of the same coin; two extremes of the same sickness.



Of course, in the United States, no social phenomenon pops up without many entrepreneurs popping up to monetise it. The new crop of “skinny influencers” are remarkably different from diet-peddlers of the past. Instagram So it is with the new thinness. The new crop of “skinny influencers” – who collectively have millions of followers, and subscriber-only clubs where women can join chat groups and see exclusive “skinny” content – are remarkably different from diet-peddlers past. Their central message is to “drop the rules” many yo-yo dieters have had around food, and to develop a “normal” relationship with it, eating everything, but just not too much of it. One such influencer recently posted about how she had been craving a cinnamon scroll. So she ordered one on Uber Eats, ate a small portion of it and then threw it away.



This influencer purports to be selling self-composure, regulation and healthy control. The skinny influencers evangelise that they can take or leave food, having a bite and then setting it down, and they claim that they can teach others this skill. The irony of creating a career around decentring food, while constantly talking about, well, food, is lost on them. Since humans were able to make images of themselves and others, certain standards of appearance have been elevated above others. Artists and romantics have always sought an ideal of beauty, and from the foot-binding of Ming Dynasty China to the corsetry of Victorian England, that ideal has often necessitated the suffering of women. But the current crop of skinny influencers are not peddling beauty, per se. They are peddling control and perhaps the related ideal of “hotness”, and it’s now spread to men who risk becoming just as strictured-by-expectation as women.



They are selling an extreme, which is the ultimate zeitgeist product. Jacqueline Maley is an author and columnist. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Perez Hilton in serious but stable condition following self-harm incident
World.content:
Graphic content CultureCelebrityMental health Perez Hilton in serious but stable condition following self-harm incident Nell Geraets August 9, 2026 — 11:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Perez Hilton is in “serious but stable condition” and will require surgery after he appeared to commit self-harm in a livestream earlier this week, according to a new statement written by his family. “He experienced significant blood loss and sustained additional injuries that will require surgery in the coming days,” Hilton’s family wrote on his website PerezHilton.com on Sunday. “His treatment and recovery will be a long process. We are grateful that Perez was able to spend time with his mother and sister yesterday.” Perez Hilton remains in hospital where he will undergo surgery in the coming days. Getty The celebrity blogger was hospitalised on August 4 after sharing a TikTok livestream in which he appeared to harm himself. Concerned viewers notified the authorities, which prompted a police response. Hilton was then hospitalised under Florida’s Baker Act – a law allowing authorities to involuntarily hold someone for a period of time if they pose a threat of harm to themselves or others. The family’s statement demanded privacy, urging members of both the media and public to stop visiting Hilton’s property.



“There is absolutely no reason for members of the media or the public to remain outside the family’s home,” the statement read. “We again respectfully ask members of the media to leave the home and surrounding area, stop following family members, and cease photographing Perez’s children. We also ask photo agencies not to purchase, publish, or distribute any photographs of the children that may have been taken.” Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s deputies visited the home where Perez Hilton was found after he appeared to harm himself during a TikTok livestream. Getty Images According to the statement, Hilton’s three children (whom he had via surrogacy) remain safe and are being cared for by immediate family. “Please allow them, and the rest of the family, the peace and privacy they desperately need during this incredibly difficult time. Thank you for your continued support, compassion and understanding.” In an earlier update, Hilton’s family said the blogger was able “to communicate”, which gave them hope.



Related Article Graphic content

Mental health Perez Hilton’s children ‘fled’ home minutes before ‘severe mental health crisis’ Since then, however, they said there had been several “false and inaccurate” reports regarding the blogger’s condition. “We want to confirm that Perez remains hospitalised under Florida’s Baker Act. His communication has been extremely limited and confined to immediate family, medical providers and others directly involved in his care.” There has been no communication between Hilton and the media, the statement continued, and he has not issued any public statements. “The only statements regarding Perez that should be considered credible and authorised are those published directly on PerezHilton.com.” On August 6, the family revealed in a separate statement that Hilton’s children and other family members had been inside the home on August 4, just minutes before the livestream began. They reportedly fled the property once it became clear he was experiencing a severe mental health crisis.



Authorities from the Miami-Dade County Sheriff’s Office attended the 48-year-old blogger’s home after receiving several calls from concerned members of the public who had seen a distressing livestream of Hilton appearing to harm himself. Hilton’s TikTok account has since been suspended. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636. Oscar Colman Related Article City to Surf Meet the Babblers: The City2Surf’s most talkative squad Holly Campbell took out the women’s race, crossing the line at Bondi in 46:35. Competing in the elite category of the race for the first time, the 30-year-old surpassed the time her twin sister Paige set when she came second two years ago. “I dreamed about winning this race as a kid,” Campbell, who grew up on a farm in central NSW, said. “Dreams do come true.”



Not everyone was taking the world’s biggest fun run so seriously. A group of four runners dressed as football referees and linesmen were “just keeping everyone in check”, with a whistle and a red card in the pocket. Not chickening out: City2Surf participants making their way towards Bondi. Oscar Colman Many more wore costumes, for a laugh or for charity. Participants have raised more than $63 million for good causes since the fundraising total was first recorded in 2008. The race began at 7.30am, but before dawn contestants had begun to gather at the start line near Hyde Park in the CBD.



Diego Soto, wearing blue-tinted aviator sunglasses, was hoping for a time below an hour. His strategy was “run fast before Heartbreak Hill”, the steep stretch between Rose Bay and Vaucluse. Another early riser, Dan Agnew, said “everybody complains about it” but he liked Heartbreak Hill. “It’s actually really cool,” said Agnew, who was also hoping for a sub-60 minute time. Jessy Bonney’s pre-race preparation included listening to “upbeat emo music” as she readied herself to draw on the crowd’s momentum. “You feel everybody’s energy for the ‘ready, set, go’, you just use it,” Bonney said. “You’re part of that bubble.” Omid Toloo said he has run the race since 1996. Oscar Colman



Personal trainer Omid Toloo said this year’s City2Surf would be his 31st and he hoped there would be many more to come. “If I last until I’m 80, I’m happy.” The Morning Edition newsletter is our guide to the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up here.

World.title: Two planes involved in near-miss while taxiing at Sydney Airport
World.content:
Two planes have been involved in a near-miss while taxiing on the runway at Sydney Airport, forcing one plane to brake suddenly and injuring a crew member.

A Qatar Airways plane and a Jetstar plane were photographed on the runway metres from each other just after 7am on Sunday.

A Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways plane on the runway at Sydney Airport on Sunday morning. Nine News

There were 180 passengers on board Jetstar flight JQ402, which was heading to the Gold Coast, when the pilot spotted a Qatar Boeing 777 aircraft next to the plane, Nine News reported. The Qatar plane did not have any passengers on board and was being towed at the time, according to the report.

The pilot applied the brakes on the Airbus A320, causing one flight attendant who was moving throughout the cabin to fall. The attendant was treated by paramedics for minor injuries. No passengers were injured.

Planes nearly collide at Sydney Airport

A Jetstar plane has been forced to make an abrupt stop on the tarmac at Sydney Airport after a near miss with another aircraft.

World.title: Skinny is the new skinny: how body extremes reflect the zeitgeist
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSocial media Opinion Skinny is the new skinny: how body extremes reflect the zeitgeist Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist August 9, 2026 — 9:30am

August 9, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has proven himself incapable, so far, of winning the unnecessary Iran war he started with his president, Donald Trump. So when he announced last month that he was going to be testing all “war fighters” in the US military for their testosterone levels, it was tempting to believe Hegseth was projecting, to use the psychological term for when someone attributes their own weaknesses to another person. Ariana Grande’s video for her song Petal has led to comments about her weight. YouTube “Under the supervision of our world-class medical professionals, war fighters age 30 and older are going to be tested annually as part of their periodic health assessment,” Hegseth said in a video posted to X, titled “The High-T Department of War”. Addressing his troops, but only the male ones, it seems, he said the military needs to “constantly look for new ways to optimise your performance … ensuring you have the right testosterone levels to operate at your absolute best”.



He said troops with low testosterone levels would be topped up with hormone replacement therapy, to restore their “natural” function. I’m no expert in military strategy, but even setting aside what such a pronouncement might do for the morale of your personnel, it seems strange to signal to your enemies that your troops might not be man enough. It also sends a strong exclusionary signal to all women in the US military, from the same man who has blocked the recommended promotions of high-ranking women and people of colour, to a disproportionate degree. As the United States polarises ever further politically, it seems the extremism in politics is jumping the fence and moving into other areas of public life – notably gender politics and the way men and women present themselves physically. As men are encouraged to looksmaxx and take peptides to get larger and more imposing, to drive their muscles into hard edges and plane their chins to strong, manly angles, women are shrinking.



The extreme of the late-noughties body positivity movement, where some unhealthy bodies were presented as celebratory and desirable, has now swung to the other end of the pendulum. “Clavicular” is the physical ideal of young men who are “looksmaxxing”. Aresna Villanueva A new kind of (possibly peptide-charged) thinness is now normal and increasingly common. We see it on red carpets and in movies and on all the celebrity Instagram accounts, usually attributed to a Pilates regime and plenty of green juice. This week, the pop star Ariana Grande drew widespread attention when she released a music video for her new song “Petal” in which she looks skeletal, the bones of her shoulders protruding like those of a famine-struck child.



Grande has shrunk herself into cartoonishly tiny proportions, and yet, the narrative of the film clip depicts a jobbing actress being repeatedly rejected by a panel of ugly studio-exec men for being “not good enough”. The video ends with Grande, in character, returning to the audition room with a chainsaw and hacking the men to bloody pieces. One minute she is cloyingly seeking their approval, the next she is massacring them: talk about extremes. Fans have taken to social media to express concern about Grande’s gaunt appearance, and it has sparked multiple think-pieces on Substack and in major newspapers about whether it’s okay to comment on women’s bodies, even when it’s under the guise of worrying about their health. Grande has this week released a statement saying she will be “taking a step back from visibility”.



It is perhaps a small consolation that men now subject themselves to this sort of body scrutiny, and they are subjected to it in the media, too. This week The Times of London published an article about the “mini-paunch” of newly anointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The article noted that Burnham is “slim and fit” and has competed in various marathons. But “despite his efforts the new PM has found attention directed to his barely there mini-paunch, somewhat unfairly dubbed the ‘Burnham belly’”. But the tone of the article was interesting – rather than fat-shaming Burnham, his problem paunch was framed as something that can happen to even the healthiest of men, and nothing terribly serious to worry about.



Related Article Opinion

Eating disorders Is it OK to mention how skinny female celebrities are getting? Again? Jacqueline Maley Columnist and senior journalist The writer shared various tips to get rid of male belly fat, if you really wanted to. By contrast, Burnham’s wife, Marie-France Van Heel, was widely critiqued online for wearing a baby blue Victoria Beckham midi-dress on her first official outing with her husband. I thought she looked great, but internet trolls did what they do to women who aren’t within the boundaries of whatever they decree is acceptable. The casual fat-shaming of a prime ministerial wife and the skinny-shaming of a famous pop star are probably two sides of the same coin; two extremes of the same sickness.



Of course, in the United States, no social phenomenon pops up without many entrepreneurs popping up to monetise it. The new crop of “skinny influencers” are remarkably different from diet-peddlers of the past. Instagram So it is with the new thinness. The new crop of “skinny influencers” – who collectively have millions of followers, and subscriber-only clubs where women can join chat groups and see exclusive “skinny” content – are remarkably different from diet-peddlers past. Their central message is to “drop the rules” many yo-yo dieters have had around food, and to develop a “normal” relationship with it, eating everything, but just not too much of it. One such influencer recently posted about how she had been craving a cinnamon scroll. So she ordered one on Uber Eats, ate a small portion of it and then threw it away.



This influencer purports to be selling self-composure, regulation and healthy control. The skinny influencers evangelise that they can take or leave food, having a bite and then setting it down, and they claim that they can teach others this skill. The irony of creating a career around decentring food, while constantly talking about, well, food, is lost on them. Since humans were able to make images of themselves and others, certain standards of appearance have been elevated above others. Artists and romantics have always sought an ideal of beauty, and from the foot-binding of Ming Dynasty China to the corsetry of Victorian England, that ideal has often necessitated the suffering of women. But the current crop of skinny influencers are not peddling beauty, per se. They are peddling control and perhaps the related ideal of “hotness”, and it’s now spread to men who risk becoming just as strictured-by-expectation as women.



They are selling an extreme, which is the ultimate zeitgeist product. Jacqueline Maley is an author and columnist. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Iran makes dramatic new demands around Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Iran makes dramatic new demands around Strait of Hormuz August 9, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Iran issued dramatic new demands around the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile. Yemen’s military attacked the country’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. Here’s a look at developments across the Middle East. People spend time at a beach as commercial vessels are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran. AP Photo/Amirhosein Khorgooi Iran says the strait won’t open until the US ‘corrects’ its behaviour Iran’s politburo-like body, the Supreme National Security Council, said the Strait of Hormuz would not open until the United States “corrects its behaviour”, issuing new demands that could shake up talks on a deal to manage the waterway.



Iran’s state broadcaster published the statement by the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the powerful Revolutionary Guard. Related Article Middle East at war Eight backflips and counting: Trump is still promising his big Iran ‘deal’ The US must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The US must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets. There was no immediate comment from the US, which has wanted an acceptable deal first on the strait before ending the blockade. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and plan on compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets. A 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week, but could be extended.



Iran has said it is close to reaching a separate deal with Oman to manage the strait, which runs between the two countries. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said they were close to reaching an agreement on navigation, “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening was contingent on other conditions, he said in remarks shared on social media, and blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the interim deal. Loading Oman, a mediator Gulf Arab country that has said relatively little on the talks, said in a statement that the discussions were ongoing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”, and condemned attacks on ships on the strait. The strait, crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, had been considered an international waterway before the war. Ship transits remain low.



Iran attacks a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, the UAE says A vessel owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned ADNOC oil and gas company was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, Emirati authorities said. The Foreign Ministry said Iran fired the missile as part of attacks on commercial shipping. Related Article Middle East at war State Department warns US citizens to be ready to leave Middle East as Iran tensions boil ADNOC said in a statement there were no casualties following the attack early on Saturday (Tehran time). The company said more than a dozen of its vessels had been attacked by missiles and drones while transiting the strait since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. One crew member had been killed and 20 others wounded, it said. ADNOC didn’t elaborate on the attack’s location or any damage.



Later, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre said a vessel east of the town of Khasab, Oman, had been struck by a projectile that caused a fire that was put out, with the vessel and crew safe. It was not clear whether this was the ADNOC incident. Related Article Opinion

Trump diplomacy Trump’s ‘short war’ is spiralling out of control. His personal failings were the trigger Rodger Shanahan Middle East and security analyst A defence deal is not aimed at any third country, Turkey says A defence agreement that Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed on Friday was not aimed against any third country, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said. It says an attack on one would be considered an attack on all three. Fidan told Turkey’s state-run Anadolu Agency that the countries did not view any state as an adversary unless it took hostile action against them: “We don’t have anything written down – nothing we’ve signed – that defines a common threat.”



Asked how the mutual defence mechanism would work, Fidan said a member would formally request help and the two countries’ assistance could range from intelligence-sharing to logistics support or the deployment of military units. The mechanism would establish a secretariat to be based in Saudi Arabia, Fidan said. He said other nations, which he did not name, had expressed interest in joining the agreement, adding that he expected Egypt, which he described as a “natural partner”, to participate “at the next stage”. Yemen’s military attacks Iran-backed Houthis The attacks were in response to the Houthis’ recent strikes in central and eastern Yemen. Colonel Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for Yemen’s military, said the attacks targeted the rebels’ “sites and capabilities” on multiple front lines, without elaborating. The escalation between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government and its backer, a Saudi-supported coalition, threatens to reignite Yemen’s civil war following a 2022 truce.

World.title: Greens propose $2.4b funding to back 'critical' marae
World.content:
The Green Party is campaigning on establishing a $2.4 billion trust dedicated to marae.

Co-leader Marama Davidson said marae were critical infrastructure and needed funding certainty to continue their work responding to weather emergencies and supporting communities.

Te Rangatiratanga Trust would be owned and governed by hapū and iwi, with $2.44 billion of government investment over four years.

There would be two funds within that: the $2 billion Te Tōtara Haemata Intergenerational Fund, dedicated to long-term investment in marae and their communities; and the $400 million Te Rākau Whakarauora Restoration Fund, which would provide immediate access to funding for urgent needs.

The trust would cost about $40 million to set up and run.

Davidson said the intergenerational fund could return between $47 million and $118 million once it had matured.

"This funding recognises that marae have been critical infrastructure for a long, long time, and supports marae to do even more."

She said marae voluntarily stepped up during weather emergencies, feeding and housing locals and tourists who needed it. The investment would ensure they were appropriately funded to do so.

"But it will also support marae to do longer-term planning, climate-resilience planning, adaptation planning, housing, social services, health services," she said.

The Greens would run nationwide wānanga to establish the trust, the two funds and governance mechanisms.

Iwi Māori would design it and decide where funding would go, Davidson said.

"This is actual tino rangatiratanga for iwi," she said.

"It might take about a year with wānanga throughout the motu to sort of figure out and design exactly how the funds will be distributed."

World.title: Youth accused of murdering Napier teen Kaea Karauria to face trial in October
World.content:
A youth charged with the murder of Napier 15-year-old Kaea Karauria is due to face trial this year.

A three-week trial has been scheduled to begin in the High Court at Palmerston North on 27 October.

The 16-year-old defendant's name has been suppressed, as have other details of the case.

Kaea died in the early hours of 11 May, 2025.

He was discovered critically injured with stab wounds on Alexander Ave in Napier by police responding to reports of disorder at a birthday party nearby.

He died at the scene despite the efforts of ambulance staff to save him.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Family Court orders no contact after father’s ‘uninhibited, dysregulated’ and abusive behaviour
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains content that may be disturbing to some readers.

When a woman's ex-partner stood outside the Family Court courtroom during proceedings, staring at her through a door window, the woman gasped, curled into a foetal position and tried to move as far away from his sight as possible.

The moment followed years of volatile behaviour, false allegations and intimidation of professionals.

A judge later described the man's conduct as "uninhibited, dysregulated, and at times, frankly abusive", both inside and outside the courtroom.

With no agency willing to supervise him and a pattern of behaviour that placed his children and former partner at ongoing risk, the court has now made the rare decision that his children have no contact with him.

The decision was released in a Family Court ruling by Judge Stephen Coyle, bringing eight years of litigation to an end. The family has automatic name suppression.

The court heard the relationship ended after a family barbecue when the man argued with others before leaving with his partner and children in the car.

During the journey home, he drove at 120km/h and the mother told the court she feared for their lives.

The incident was recorded and played to the judge, who noted it was "a distressing incident to watch".

The man was heard saying, "You know what I'm f***ing capable of, I'll go for your dad's f***ing throat",** and telling everyone to shut up when asked to stop.

When they got home, the woman said he did a doughnut in the driveway and drove at speed towards the carport before abruptly stopping.

He took the woman's phone and, as she was crying, she said he licked her tears and said: "Hmmm, I love the way they taste."

The woman later applied for a temporary protection order (TPO) and an interim parenting order with supervised access, which were granted. But the TPO was not made final and was discharged a year later.

Months later, unsupervised access was granted to the father but, in 2022, he alleged his children were being sexually abused and did not return them.

The woman applied for a warrant to enforce the parenting order and the children were returned to her care.

Oranga Tamariki (OT) investigated the allegations and found no evidence of abuse, but the father continued raising his concerns with authorities.

In December 2022, the father took one of the children to an emergency department alleging she had suffered a head injury, but staff became concerned about his behaviour.

He reportedly yelled at a nurse, telling her to "f*** off", and a report of concern was made to OT.

OT visited the father days later and reported he was agitated and unable to hold a direct line of conversation. The social workers became frightened by his presentation and left.

He again refused to return the children and the mother had to file another application for a warrant, which was granted.

The same day, the man had taken the girls to a police station to report the allegations of abuse.

Oranga Tamariki (OT) investigated the allegations and found no evidence of abuse from the mother, but the father continued raising his concerns with authorities. NZME / Supplied

Unbeknownst to him, the warrant had been issued for the children to be uplifted, and police executed it at the station.

"This was not a straightforward process. [The father] was understandably upset that the warrant had been granted given his belief that the girls were at risk in their mother's care," Judge Coyle said in the decision.

"He had to be arrested by the police and removed so that [the children] could be returned to their mother's care."

After being released, he turned up to an OT office and when staff became afraid, he was removed and a trespass order was issued.

He then called 111 and claimed his children had been taken.

School concerns

According to the decision, the children's school gave evidence to the Family Court that it became concerned about the father's behaviour, particularly when he turned up to a "funky fun day" event and took photos of children and staff.

He then posted the photos online with derogatory comments and the school implemented a lockdown policy if he was sighted near the school.

The mother was granted another interim protection order, which became final when the man did not file any opposition.

She was also granted a further variation of the parenting order, reinstating supervised access for the father.

But supervised contact could not proceed because the provider terminated its contract due to his behaviour.

He then filed an application seeking day-to-day care and the discharge of the parenting order, which proceeded to a hearing.

Several delays occurred before the eight-day hearing, including the father failing to file evidence and two assigned senior lawyers withdrawing from acting for him.

Lawyer Michael Roots was eventually assigned and Judge Coyle commended his role.

"My observation was that Mr Roots showed enormous forbearance in the face of, at times, rude and belligerent attacks by [the father]."

Court behaviour

The judge found that during the cross-examination of the mother, the father used the process to psychologically abuse her.

For days, the man routinely interrupted the judge and would loudly interrupt his lawyer with questions he wanted asked of the woman.

"During the last session of the first day of the hearing I had to ask [the father] to leave the courtroom as his behaviour in court had become untenable," the decision said.

"He did so, but then stood at the door peering into the courtroom through the window and was staring directly at [the mother] and in doing so he was breaching the protection order.

"When she saw him [as the screen used did not shield her from that view] she instantly gasped, scooted in her chair as far away as she could in the witness box, curled up into the foetal position on the chair, and stated, 'He's staring, I mean he's just right there in the doorway'."

The judge described her distress as instinctive and visceral.

At the hearing, the father claimed he was the victim of family violence at the hands of the woman, but the judge ruled he had no evidence to support the allegations.

Judge Coyle said that when questioned about the barbecue incident, the man claimed his ex-partner was drunk and that he had been acting in self-defence.

"His evidence was chilling in his attempt to blame her. The video speaks for itself," the judge said.

"His language towards her was abusive and dismissive, he essentially tried to shut her down so that she had no voice or agency in her distress. It was behaviour designed to belittle, antagonise, frighten, demean and diminish [the mother].

"There is no evidence that [the mother] was drunk as asserted by [the father]. He is simply making that up in an attempt to victim-blame."

Intimidating professionals

The court also heard evidence that Family Court staff had been reduced to tears by the man's behaviour, particularly a senior Family Court practitioner.

"There are patterns in relation to [the father's] interactions with virtually every person or agency he has come into contact with which have caused people to be concerned for their physical and/or psychological safety.

"My assessment therefore is that there is an extremely high risk of future family harm to [the mother] in particular if the protection order was discharged."

The judge directed the protection order be made final and made a rare order granting sole care of the children to the mother with no contact for the father.

"His behaviour in court, at a time in which [the father] should have been on his best behaviour while the gaze of the court was on him, was uninhibited, dysregulated, and at times, frankly abusive and intimidating," Judge Coyle said.

"In order to protect [the children], there could only be supervised contact with [the father]. But there is no agency willing to supervise [his] contact with these girls.

"I therefore have determined that an order should be made that [the children] are to have no contact with [the father]."

The judge also ruled the man's behaviour amounted to litigant abuse and ordered that he not file any new proceedings against his ex-partner for three years.
